On MATH, Prune-to-Probe reduces reasoning-token forwards by 2.60%, preserving all naturally correct trajectories while repairing six errors. On MMLU-Pro, it achieves 1.145% pooled savings with no observed harm. Further analysis shows that the intervention captures decision stability rather than correctness (AUROC 0.502). These results demonstrate the potential of causal activation probes for efficient inference-time control without permanent model modification.
item.dc:creator: Yufei Qi, Chonghe Jiang

item.title: ProtLink: Sequence and Multispecies Graph Context for Protein Interaction Prediction
item.description: Predicting protein-protein interactions (PPIs) from sequence alone is difficult, while known interaction networks may provide informative biological context. We introduce ProtLink, a sequence-conditioned graph-learning framework that combines frozen ESM-2 representations with protein interaction topology and orthogroup-mediated connections between species. We compare sequence-only models, GraphSAGE, a homogeneous graph transformer, and a heterogeneous graph transformer (HGT) for human PPI prediction. In an initial edge-level comparison, three-layer multispecies HGT with ESM-2 650M features achieves an average precision (AP) of 0.980 under random negative sampling, compared with 0.951 for the homogeneous transformer; its AP decreases to 0.878 with two-hop-preferred negatives. In controlled three-seed experiments, three-layer full-graph HGT obtains an AP of $0.9701\pm0.0022$, exceeding an orthogroup-only model ($0.9435\pm0.0094$). The corresponding two-layer comparison shows little additional benefit from non-human PPI edges, consistent with the greater message-passing depth needed to transmit their information. For human proteins excluded from training interactions, multispecies HGT achieves $0.8335\pm0.0094$ AP versus $0.6482\pm0.0052$ for a sequence-only pair model. These results identify the value, depth dependence, and limits of evolutionary graph context while distinguishing prediction of held-out edges from generalization to held-out proteins.
item.dc:creator: Xingyuan Zhang

item.title: DPDP: Diffusion Policy-Steered Diffusion Planner for Offline Reinforcement Learning
item.description: In offline reinforcement learning, diffusion models fill two roles with complementary strengths. Typically guided by a critic, a diffusion policy is value-aware and favors high-return, behavior-supported actions, but it is short-sighted: it never lays out the states it intends to visit. A diffusion planner is far-sighted, synthesizing such a long-horizon trajectory, but it is only behavior-driven at execution, realizing each planned transition using only offline behavior.Each is strong exactly where the other is weak. We introduce DPDP to bring them together at the planner's execution step, where a planned transition becomes an action. Reading the planner's inverse-dynamics executor as a posterior over actions: the environment's transition likelihood relates an action to the planned next state, while the behavioral prior determines its weight under the offline data. Replacing this prior with a value-optimized diffusion policy preserves the planned transition likelihood and favors valuable actions that can serve the plan. We target the resulting clean-action distribution in two ways. A training-free sampler composes policy and inverse-dynamics scores at matched action noise levels and applies Langevin correction; this route uses a shared action noise schedule and an approximately common terminal prior. A preference objective instead amortizes the transfer into a single diffusion executor. Across D4RL, DPDP improves the planner it builds on, staying competitive with reactive diffusion policies on locomotion and leading on long-horizon navigation.
item.dc:creator: Ruyi An, Mingyuan Zhou

item.title: An Analysis of Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation
item.description: We address the problem of computing the optimal Q-function in Markov decision problems with infinite state-space. We analyze the convergence properties of several variations of Q-learning when combined with function approximation, extending the analysis of TD-learning in Tsitsiklis and Van Roy (1996) to stochastic control settings. We identify conditions under which such approximate methods converge with probability 1. We conclude with a brief discussion on the general applicability of our results and compare them with several related works.
item.dc:creator: Francisco S. Melo, Sean P. Meyn, M. Isabel Ribeiro

item.title: Optimal Byzantine-resilient Federated Learning with User-level Differential Privacy
item.description: Real-world deployment of federated learning (FL) requires resilience against adversarial clients and data privacy. Byzantine fault captures the worst-case behavior of adversarial clients, while differential privacy (DP) provides statistical guarantees against privacy loss. In particular, user-level DP guards a client's entire contribution and provides more realistic protection against information leakage. Despite intensive efforts, the minimax-optimal convergence bound of Byzantine-resilient FL with user-level DP remains open. We establish an information-theoretic lower bound for any Byzantine-resilient empirical risk minimization problem under user-level DP and heterogeneous clients. We propose ByzULDP, a central DP algorithm featuring a two-level momentum across the client and server. Client-side momentum mitigates stochastic gradient variance during robust aggregation. Unlike the fault-free case, naively combining non-linear Byzantine-resilient aggregation with central DP noise can be insufficient to guarantee convergence to a bounded neighborhood of a stationary point. Our key contribution is a server-side momentum that leverages a property specific to user-level DP, where privacy sensitivity depends on how client updates are constructed, to empower convergence. ByzULDP achieves the order-optimal convergence bound for strongly-convex objectives, with vanishing error terms decaying at the optimal $O(1/T)$ and $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rates for strongly-convex and non-convex objectives, respectively. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments on real-world datasets across diverse privacy budgets.
item.dc:creator: Ming Xiang, Stratis Ioannidis, Edmund Yeh, Carlee Joe-Wong, Lili Su

item.title: Stochastic Port-Hamiltonian Gaussian Processes for Learning from Noisy Dynamics on Lie Groups
item.description: Learning predictive models for dynamics is difficult because observations are often sparse and noisy, while the underlying dynamics evolve on nonlinear configuration manifolds and are affected by environmental dissipation and stochastic disturbances. Standard neural dynamics models can fit short-term trajectories but often violate physical structure, accumulate error over long horizons, or rely on parameterizations that introduce singularities such as gimbal lock. We introduce LieSPHGP, a stochastic Gaussian-process framework for learning rigid body dynamics with port-Hamiltonian structure and stability-aware robustness. LieSPHGP represents motion on Lie groups and Lie algebras, enabling coordinate-consistent optimization without singular parameterizations. Learned mass, potential energy, dissipation, and control components retain physical roles and a separate diffusion term represents stochastic forcing. Each component is modeled by Mat\'ern kernel Gaussian processes which capture uncertainty induced by noisy observations. To improve physical validity, Lie group exponential map updates preserve rotational constraints, while positive-definite damping ensures nonnegative deterministic energy dissipation. The implicit-explicit integrator additionally provides unconditional stability for the frozen linear damping subsystem. The resulting model learns predictive dynamics that are robust to noise, respect rigid body geometry, and capture both intrinsic motion and environmental dissipation. Experiments on various noisy rigid body benchmarks show improved prediction accuracy, stronger long-horizon stability, and better satisfaction of manifold constraints compared with neural dynamics baselines. Code, data and interactive results are available on the project website: https://thribhuvanrapolu.github.io/liesphgp/
item.dc:creator: Thribhuvan Rapolu, Luke McLennan, Chandrajit Bajaj

item.title: SWXAI: A Unified Multimodal Explainability Library for Space Weather Forecasting and Heliophysics
item.description: Space weather forecasting and heliophysics increasingly rely on machine learning models that process heterogeneous inputs such as multi-viewpoint multi-wavelength solar images and rasters, multivariate time series, spatial annotations, and tabular event-level data. However, explainability workflows remain fragmented across libraries, model interfaces, and output formats, limiting reuse and reproducibility. We present SWXAI, an open-source library that unifies explainable AI (XAI) workflows for image, time-series, and tabular data in space weather forecasting and heliophysics. SWXAI provides a common, extensible interface across commonly used vision, time-series, and tabular learning models, with validation, adaptation, and persistent explanation objects. It also includes domain-grounded examples, reproducible notebooks, tests, and documentation, enabling users to inspect outputs, swap models or explainers, and extend workflows to new heliophysics datasets. SWXAI reduces modality-specific engineering overhead and supports comparable, reusable explanations across heterogeneous scientific machine learning pipelines. A benchmark against direct backend implementations shows that SWXAI substantially reduces the code users write to produce an explanation, with no practical runtime cost.
item.dc:creator: Benedict Antonio Mervyn, Anli Ji, Manolis K. Georgoulis, Berkay Aydin

item.title: Meta-Reinforcement Learning with Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning
item.description: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) trains agents to adapt to novel tasks from test-time experience, but requires diverse training environments and reward functions. While environments are becoming cheaper to generate, it remains difficult to anticipate every objective an agent may be asked to pursue at test time. Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) learn policies from reward-free data and support zero-shot RL (ZSRL): adaptation to new objectives at test time using a large reward-labeled dataset. Recent work has shown that BFM task inference can instead be performed online without prior task-specific data. We note that this capability positions BFMs and meta-RL as alternative approaches for online adaptation to new reward functions in a fixed environment. We then ask whether we can extend BFMs to compete with meta-RL more broadly, including in novel environments, and identify four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and learning from mixed reward supervision. We study each individually, then propose MetaBFM, a hybrid method that addresses all four. During training, it combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning; at test time, it can interpolate between exploration, exploitation, and ZSRL-style reward inference. We demonstrate that MetaBFM can recover the in-distribution performance of supervised meta-RL while generalizing to reward functions outside the training set. Our work suggests that BFMs and meta-RL are complementary research directions whose combined strengths allow adaptive agents to learn more diverse behaviors from a fixed set of supervised objectives.
item.dc:creator: Jake Grigsby, Siddhant Agarwal, Yu Lei, Leonidas Varveropoulos, Yuke Zhu

item.title: Regularization Amplifies Subliminal Learning
item.description: Recent work has shown that hidden biases can be transferred through data with no apparent semantic relationship to those biases. Can regularization limit this covert influence? By constraining adaptation, regularization might be expected to suppress behavioral changes on seemingly unrelated inputs. We systematically study this hypothesis in subliminal learning, as well as in related settings of covert influence, including phantom transfer and logit-linear selection. We find the opposite: regularization amplifies the transfer of hidden biases. In particular, subliminal learning is typically absent under full fine-tuning, but low-rank adaptation or explicit penalties can induce strong transfer. Phantom transfer and logit-linear selection show similar trends. Adding more data, an implicit form of regularization, also strengthens covert influence. Together, these findings suggest that the simplicity biases induced by regularization may facilitate covert influence. We further hypothesize that the level of regularization that maximizes covert transfer depends on task complexity.
item.dc:creator: Lawrence Feng, Jacob Mitchell Springer, Gaurav R. Ghosal, Ziqian Zhong, Aditi Raghunathan

item.title: Finite Time Analysis of Risk-Sensitive RL via Noisy Power Iteration
item.description: Estimating the principal eigenpair of a positive operator from stochastic evaluations gives rise to a noisy form of normalized power iteration: each step applies a sampled operator estimate and then renormalizes. We establish finite-time stochastic-approximation guarantees for this procedure, working in Hilbert's projective metric, which is well-suited to the multiplicative geometry of Perron--Frobenius eigenproblems. Our main application is risk-sensitive average-cost reinforcement learning (RL) with exponential utility. In this setting the Bellman equations are multiplicative, and value functions are characterized by nonlinear eigenvalue problems rather than additive fixed points. We cast both policy evaluation and control in this framework, obtaining risk-sensitive TD- and Q-learning algorithms that learn from a single Markovian trajectory. Under explicit positivity, mixing, and linear function approximation assumptions, we prove finite-time bounds on the recovered eigenvector and eigenvalue with $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity up to problem-dependent constants. The results cover both tabular and linear function approximation regimes, and through the duality between exponential utility and KL-robust control yield finite-time guarantees for KL-robust average-cost RL as well.
item.dc:creator: Waqar Mirza, Yashaswini Murthy, Laixi Shi, Eric Mazumdar, Adam Wierman

item.title: Bias, Measurement Error, and Double-Dipping: When Can GNN Convolutions Help Brain Connectome Prediction?
item.description: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are an important tool for fMRI prediction, where empirical functional connectivity matrices serve both as features and for graph construction. However, recent studies and our own experiments show that these methods often fail to outperform simpler graph-agnostic baselines. We propose a statistical explanation for this failure by formulating connectome prediction as an errors-in-variables (EIV) problem: the true connectome is latent, while the observed covariance matrix is a noisy finite-time-series estimate. In a linear asymptotic setting, we decompose the effect of graph convolution into three mechanisms: smoothing-induced bias and variance reduction, graph estimation error, and a double-dipping effect arising when the same noisy matrix determines both graph and features. Under a latent community model adapted to neuroscience, we identify a narrow favorable regime, set by the brain community structure, the predictive signal, the graph construction and the recording length, in which message passing can improve prediction. Simulations validate this decomposition, while real-data experiments illustrate that connectome GNN pipelines often fall outside this regime. Our results provide a first step towards explaining when graph convolutions can help brain connectome prediction, and why they often do not.
item.dc:creator: Tommaso Castellani, Jiaqi Li, Muriah D. Wheelock, Rezwana Rosen Razzaque, Helmut Laufs, Hong Chen, Claire Donnat

item.title: Plug-and-Play Verifier for Decoupling Process Reward in Stabilizing Long-Horizon Agentic Reasoning
item.description: Stabilizing long-horizon reasoning requires intelligent agents to sustain useful progress across successive reasoning steps and tool interactions. Such agents are typically trained with reinforcement learning (RL), where actor-critic RL uses a learnable critic network to estimate step advantages, while critic-free methods such as GRPO eliminate critic models and rely mostly on the group variants of sparse outcome-only rewards. Both reward types leave partially useful failed trajectories either implicit or indistinguishable from entirely unproductive ones, and as reasoning horizons grow, it becomes difficult to maintain consistent reasoning trajectories. In this work, we propose a \textit{plug-and-play verifier} framework for stabilizing long-horizon reasoning through explicit verification of intermediate reasoning artifacts. Specifically, the framework decouples process verification through a unified interface that extracts intermediate reasoning artifacts from agent running trajectories, evaluates them using domain-specific verifiers, and aggregates the verification scores as bounded process reward. Then, we combine our dense verified process rewards and the sparse outcome rewards through a two-stage post-training schedule. We showed that with plug-and-play verifiers, we further stabilize the reasoning steps as last-mile self-reflection and self-consistency. Typical evaluation on HotpotQA using Qwen3.5-4B achieves a superior accuracy (60.18\%), outperforming the standard GRPO baseline (57.73\%). Our results suggest that plug-and-play verifiers provide a modular approach to learn more stable and reliable reasoning behaviors over long horizons.
item.dc:creator: Mingwei Xu, Jieyuan Pei, Binghao Tu, Hao Fang

item.title: Fast Accurate Quantum Monte Carlo without Metropolis Adjustment
item.description: In quantum systems, physical quantities of interest can be expressed as expectation values of a probability distribution, which allows their estimation by Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. This approach, an instance of Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC), plays a central role in obtaining predictions of system properties relevant to condensed matter and high energy physics. The use of Hamiltonian dynamics to design a Markov kernel, known as Hybrid or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), is widespread in quantum applications. In this context, it is standard to use an HMC kernel that is ``adjusted'' with the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) criterion, so that estimates of expectations converge to their true value in the limit of infinite sample size. However, recent work in computational statistics suggests that an \emph{unadjusted} HMC kernel can be significantly more efficient, while safely maintaining an asymptotic bias which is small relative to the error arising from the variance of the finite sample size. We adapt this approach to the QMC setting, focusing on a challenging and high-dimensional \emph{spin-fermion} model of a quantum phase transition. We find that unadjusted methods outperform adjusted HMC in terms of effective sample size per gradient call, while retaining accurate results.
item.dc:creator: Reuben Cohn-Gordon, Gabriel Pescia, Sumner N. Hearth, Jakob Robnik, Uro\v{s} Seljak, Peter Lunts

item.title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients
item.description: Users are asking language models mental health questions and are receiving answers. We audited what 41 language models recommend to users when the same clinical information reaches them from three footings: a clinician describing a patient, a caregiver describing a loved one, or a person describing themselves. Across 19 case vignettes and five questions, we collected 35,055 free-text responses, extracted every intervention named with a validated judge, and had 29 models rate the full option lists on a seven-point Likert scale for the same cases. Models largely recommend what they rate well, with recommendation behavior differing by footing, and many models offering clinicians a consultation-style response and lay users hedged, simplified advice. When asked about recommendations for a specific intervention type, models more often named options they themselves rated below zero as initial choices, usually with conditions attached. We will release the instrument, code, and full corpus on publication as a living audit.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Flathers, Jill Noorily, Phuong Anh Nguyen, Mark Kalinich, Mina Fallah, Victoria Lisowski, Christine Shi, Rebekah M. Bodner, Anna Simms, Mihika Hete, Meiting Chen, Samuel K. Powell, Tatum Williamson, Laura Ospina-Pinillos, Haruka Notsu, Julian Herpertz, John Torous

item.title: When Calibration Data Matter in Sub-4-Bit Language Model Quantization
item.description: Low-bit post-training quantization reduces language-model memory but can sharply degrade downstream task accuracy. Calibration usually relies on generic text, but when task-informed data recover accuracy and which quantizers benefit remain poorly understood. We introduce FragCal-DC, which supplements generic text with training documents from task families with low retention of full-precision accuracy in a two-bit scan. We use a two- to four-bit sweep to locate functional regimes and four-seed calibration comparisons to evaluate six data-dependent methods across six dense models (1.7B-8B) and ten tasks. At their lowest tested functional bit widths, iterative SignRound V2 and OmniQuant improve at two bits, whereas single-pass GPTQ and AWQ show small mean responses at three bits. At two bits, SignRound V2 gains 1.83 percentage points in mean ten-task accuracy over generic-text calibration across six models. At 70 billion parameters, GPTQ and SignRound V2 both improve at two bits, with functional generic-calibration baselines. For two-bit SignRound V2, task-level controls show that recovery concentrates on families included in calibration, while incorrect answer designations retain about 90% of the mean accuracy gain. Changes in reconstruction error do not consistently track accuracy gains. These findings support task-informed calibration as a design principle for preserving downstream accuracy in low-bit quantization.
item.dc:creator: Yehong Jiang, Yen-Kuang Chen, Xinmin Tian

item.title: Collaboration Signatures: Tracking Long-Horizon Dynamics of Cross-Meeting Collaboration Networks
item.description: Enterprise platforms have received increasing attention as a core component of social networks and the Web. However, existing work mostly relies on fragmented logs of small units of work, like emails and chats, and focuses on who connects with whom without sufficient account of collaboration content and dynamics. This work systematically explores tracking collaborations across sequences of meetings as a new approach to interpreting their long-horizon dynamics. Linking 45,426 meetings in a large multinational technology company based on full transcripts and 1.6 million extracted agenda items, we establish a cross-meeting collaboration network of 6,065 collaborations. The network recovers the natural shapes of workplace collaborations: meetings, as snapshots of ongoing collaboration, link into largely tree-shaped structures, while the work content forms nested directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Further, we explore how these networks evolve over time, examining three established perspectives: task division, team composition, and temporal continuity. Each explains part of the dynamics but does not capture the distinctness of long-horizon workplace collaboration: e.g., work flows in a consistent direction between a few pairs of subjects, yet a collaboration's subject explains little of how its meetings are conducted. Instead, accumulating the agenda, interaction, and language of meetings along each tree yields a signature of the collaboration, a distinctive profile that picks out the collaboration of a held-out meeting at 4.5 times chance. The signature models collaboration better than team or task views, individually or combined, in next-meeting prediction and tree-level fitting. We discuss the implications of these cross-meeting dynamics for designing office applications and support tools, and call for next-generation Web systems that represent collaborations over their long horizon.
item.dc:creator: Shengqi Zhu, Sheshera Mysore, Bahareh Sarrafzadeh

item.title: How Much Is Left Matters: False Positives and False Negatives in Partial-Prompt Contamination Tests
item.description: Partial-prompt completion, where a model receives the first part of a benchmark problem and is checked for whether it reproduces the rest, is a widely used test for benchmark contamination. We audit this test on seven open-weight models using MATH-500 and recent AIME 2025/2026 problems, which serve as true negatives. Memorization flags depend strongly on how much text remains: for every model, problems with at most 8 leftover words are flagged several times more often than problems with at least 25 (31.5% vs. 5.5% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), and half to three-quarters of all ROUGE-based flags come from short leftovers. On true negatives, a ROUGE-L >= 0.75 threshold flags up to 6.7% of problems at a 60% prefix, and at an 80% prefix even exact match flags 8.6% (pooled over models; 6.2% on AIME 2026, which postdates every model), against 0% at 40-60%. The test also misses contamination upstream: models distilled from Qwen2.5-Math, whose base is heavily flagged in prior work, show almost no model-specific recall. Calibrating each model against models from other families removes most flags while isolating a consistent Qwen2.5-specific signal at every prefix length. We recommend length-stratified reporting, prefixes of at most 60%, style-matched post-cutoff controls, and cross-family calibration.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek Anand

item.title: Is Persona Generalization Predictable?
item.description: Persona generalization occurs when fine-tuning a language model in one domain induces behavioral changes in others -- for example, the broadly unsafe behavior observed in emergent misalignment. We discover a surprising "on-the-line" phenomenon in persona generalization: in-domain and out-of-domain persona rates across various fine-tuning hyperparameters follow an approximately probit-linear relationship, and the specific probit-linear relationship is surprisingly shared even across model families and model sizes, including Qwen and Llama. Training choices that leave the set of trainable parameters unchanged, such as learning rate, weight decay, and training duration, largely move models along the same line, reducing transfer mainly by weakening in-domain learning. Changing which layers are fine-tuned, however, can change the slope. For unsafe behavior, fine-tuning only later layers yields shallower slopes, retaining strong in-domain learning while reducing out-of-domain misalignment. This "on-the-line" phenomenon unifies unexpected, isolated observations of persona generalization within a quantitative framework for predicting and controlling behavioral transfer.
item.dc:creator: Olina Mukherjee, Arnav Goel, Aditi Raghunathan, Jacob Mitchell Springer

item.title: A Lattice-Based HMM Approach to Aruz Scansion of Ottoman Poetry
item.description: Ottoman Divan poetry is composed in aruz, a quantitative meter based on the weights of syllables. The meter is sensitive to specific characters recorded in the original writing in the Arabic script. This work is concerned with automatic meter finding and scansion alignment for Ottoman Divan poetry, especially on modern Turkish spelling without the special diacritics that scholarly transliterations of Ottoman preserve. We define two tasks on this input, first identifying the meter used in the poem, and second aligning the meter's weights with the syllabification of the poem, identifying the flaws and freedoms the poet has taken along the way. We build a corpus of 52,000 lines split by poet, with scansion annotations for 500 test lines, and a robustness benchmark generated at the deviation rates measured on real web and OCR copies. Our model is a hidden Markov model over the positions of each meter, decoded over a lattice of every candidate path, and trained by EM from the printed meter, without scansion labels. On a held-out set it scans 77.6% of the test lines fully correctly, against 26.8% for the available rule-based scanner, 55.0% for a neural tagger trained with the same supervision and 63.6% for Claude Opus 5.5 few-shot. The code is open-sourced and the tool is released on the web.
item.dc:creator: Mehmet Emre Tiryaki

item.title: Path-Level Structural and Semantic Alignment for Hierarchical Multi-Label Text Classification
item.description: Hierarchical multi-label text classification (HMTC) requires models to capture both structural dependencies among labels and the fine-grained semantics of labels at different hierarchy levels. Existing methods often model hierarchy through prediction constraints or representations of individual labels and local relations. Structural and semantic supervision, however, are usually formulated separately. We instead use complete root-to-node label paths as a shared unit for both. Our framework introduces two auxiliary training objectives while retaining a standard multi-label classifier at inference. PathSimNCE aligns document representations with hierarchical paths using hierarchy-aware contrastive targets. These targets provide graded supervision for structurally related paths while preserving explicit supervision for the ground-truth paths. The complementary semantic objective uses LLM-generated, document-conditioned descriptions of the same positive paths. It thereby provides context-specific label semantics beyond static label representations. Experiments on three benchmarks show consistent improvements: structural alignment is particularly beneficial in deeper hierarchies, while semantic alignment provides additional gains for fine-grained labels.
item.dc:creator: Xindi Wang, Aifen Xiong, Baiyang Wang, Xuri Ge, Robert Mercer, Frank Rudzicz, Yifan Peng, Zhumin Chen, Hongjun Wang

item.title: MNN-Pocket-0.3B Technical Report
item.description: This technical report presents MNN-Pocket-0.3B, a compact 300M-parameter dense language model designed for efficient on-device deployment and supporting context lengths of up to 32K tokens. With an INT4 deployment footprint of only 173 MB and decoding throughput of up to 466 tokens/s on iPad Pro M5 (Metal), it can be seamlessly integrated into applications on edge devices such as smartphones and smart glasses. MNN-Pocket-0.3B is developed through the co-design of its architecture, data, training pipeline, and inference system. Hardware-aware architecture selection and dependency-aware vocabulary pruning balance model capability with on-device memory and compute constraints. A four-stage pre-training pipeline covering approximately 4.1 trillion high-quality Chinese and English tokens equips the model with broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. This is followed by a three-stage post-training pipeline comprising instruction fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and quantization-aware training. Finally, hardware-specific optimizations in the MNN inference engine enable fast, memory-efficient inference and long-context processing. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MNN-Pocket-0.3B achieves frontier-level performance among models of comparable size, with particularly strong results in Chinese and English knowledge and reasoning, mathematics, coding, and instruction following. It consistently outperforms similarly sized open-source models and even surpasses several 0.5B-parameter models on instruction-following benchmarks. We release MNN-Pocket-0.3B with open weights and ready-to-use MNN deployment packages. We hope it will provide a practical foundation for capable, responsive, and memory-efficient edge applications while advancing research and development in on-device language models.
item.dc:creator: MNN Team

item.title: Improving Confidence Estimation in Language Models with Linear Representations of Ambiguity
item.description: As language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed in downstream applications, accurately estimating their likelihood of success on a given example is critical. However, confidence estimates from LMs are poor predictors of their likelihood of success. Accurate confidence estimation is linked in part to the detection of aleatoric uncertainty; we hypothesize that LMs possess representations of at least some aspects of this uncertainty in the form of representations of the inherent ambiguity of the input. Using difference-in-means on minimal pairs of ambiguous and unambiguous sentences, we derive ambiguity representations in LM activations, and find that steering with them selectively (albeit weakly) modulates LMs' judgments of the input's ambiguity. We then propose DART, a fine-tuning method that encourages updates to lie within the span of the ambiguity directions, and penalizes changes to the LM activations outside of this subspace. DART greatly improves calibration, encodes these improvements into the model parameters, and maintains model accuracy on multiple-choice and generative QA tasks.
item.dc:creator: Themistoklis Nikas, Nishant Subramani, Aaron Mueller

item.title: Beyond the Transcript: Measuring and Improving the Use of Acoustic Information in Audio Language Models
item.description: Audio language model benchmarks provide comprehensive evaluation across diverse tasks. However, some tasks can be answered from the transcript or even the question alone, and benchmark scores can therefore confound acoustic understanding with language modeling ability. We distinguish lexical tasks, for which the transcript usually suffices, from global-attribute and within-recording-structure tasks, which require the model to analyse the recording beyond its words, either as a whole, for properties such as the speaker and emotion, or within it, for patterns such as stress and intonation. We evaluated 19 open models and Gemini 3.1 Pro on 92 tasks from 6 benchmarks and estimated the recording gain, the accuracy advantage of the original recording over references that retain its words, by comparing the recording with synthetic readings of its transcript and by adding it to the transcript. On attribute and structure tasks, the open models fall behind Gemini by 28.6 and 41.9 percentage points, and about half or more of each deficit lies in the recording gain. Nevertheless, linear probes in Gemma-4 12B and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B show that the acoustic information needed for answering is already readable in early language-model layers, while the readout of many cues declines in the layers that follow. We therefore constructed training data and trained LoRA adapters in these layers, with a content anchor, which raises attribute and structure accuracy by 12.8 to 44.4 points in the two models and keeps mean lexical accuracy within 1 point of the base model. Most of the improvement appears as larger recording gains. These results suggest that training improves the use of acoustic information that the models already encode.
item.dc:creator: Linkai Peng, Baorian Nuchged, Yuyang Yao

item.title: LongCap: Hour-Scale Timestamped Audio Captioning via Chunk-wise Processing
item.description: Describing hours of audio requires accurate event timing and sustained descriptive detail throughout the recording. We present LongCap, a framework for timestamped audio captioning (TAC), with the human-annotated LongCapBench and three diarization-inspired metrics: Timeline Error Rate (TER), Granularity Error Rate (GER), and Caption Similarity (tcpCapSim). LongCap interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and retained context to support length extrapolation within a 1M-token inference context window. Event-level reannotation restores caption detail, while systematic studies examine model scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation. LongCap-Diar achieves strong benchmark results and extrapolates to 16 hours of concatenated audio despite training on recordings no longer than 40 minutes. Our TAC models are competitive with Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus on short clips, outperform evaluated baselines in caption similarity and timeline accuracy in segment-level comparisons on LongCapBench-TAC-Long, and caption full recordings approaching two hours. On LongCapBench-TAC, 9B and 35B-A3B offer favorable size-performance tradeoffs, while 122B-A10B substantially improves event-dependency recovery. These findings support long-horizon general audio understanding and provide a foundation for always-on voice agents.
item.dc:creator: Jinchuan Tian, Sen Chen, Wenbin Huang, Chao Weng, Zhengwei Huang, Jiatong Shi, Yichen Lu, Haoran Wang, Shinji Watanabe, Cong Zhou

item.title: Open Problems in Chatbots and Mental Health
item.description: General-purpose chatbots are increasingly used for emotional and mental health support. They can be useful, but issues such as sycophancy, reinforcement of delusional beliefs, and poor crisis response create risks that are difficult for researchers to study and evaluate. In this paper, we review the most critical open problems for researchers and policymakers in the use of general-purpose chatbots and their effects on mental health. First, there are tractable problems in the controlled evaluation of chatbots: establishing the construct and ecological validity of evaluations, evaluating multi-turn interactions, and connecting evaluations to improvements in chatbot behavior. For example, conventional benchmarks that primarily rely on static datasets cannot establish chatbot safety, and novel simulation methods need validation. Second, researchers must connect their studies of chatbots and mental health to real-world evidence. This includes analyzing the chatbot products that AI companies and mental health practitioners have deployed, including their user interfaces and human review and escalation practices for user welfare concerns. However, clinical analysis opportunities afforded by real chat log data sharing are complicated by significant privacy concerns. Finally, we argue that researchers should take an active role in the construction and refinement of evidence-based policy through corporate and governmental decisions such as user protections, standards of care, protected access to user chat logs, data sharing between institutions, incident reporting, and post-deployment monitoring. Such behavioral evaluations, studies of real-world outcomes, and data governance depend on each other and must be addressed in tandem. We believe a coordinated research effort would have substantial real-world impact.
item.dc:creator: Jared Moore, Jacy Reese Anthis, William Agnew, Andrea Mock, Kevin Klyman, Sanmi Koyejo, Nick Haber, Stevie Chancellor, Eric Lin, Ryan Louie, Desmond C. Ong

item.title: SWEET: Mitigating Spurious Feature Reliance in LLM Reasoning via Weight Editing
item.description: Reasoning in large language models can be disrupted by simple input perturbations (e.g. adding irrelevant distractors), suggesting reliance on spurious correlations. Identifying and suppressing the spurious features involved in long chain-of-thought reasoning remains challenging. We introduce Spurious-feature WEight EdiTing (SWEET), a training-free method that combines counterfactual interventions with mechanistic interpretability to identify and suppress spurious-features. SWEET extracts token- and sequence-level behavioral directions from activation contrasts between original problems and their counterfactual variants - capturing local and global patterns of spurious reasoning. It then localizes the responsible MLP neurons and attention heads and suppresses their contributions along these directions through weight edits. Using only 20 original-counterfactual pairs for direction extraction, SWEET improves accuracy by an average of 11.8 percentage points on perturbed inputs and 2 points on original inputs across five open-weight reasoning models and five reasoning benchmarks. It also reduces the relative gap between original and perturbed accuracies from 17.6% to 2.5%. Analyses identify two recurring forms of spurious reasoning, i.e. over-integrating irrelevant conditions and overthinking, and provide mechanistic evidence that SWEET improves reasoning robustness by suppressing both behavioral directions.
item.dc:creator: Zhizhang Fu, Lucas Zhao, Michalis Korakakis, Mengru Ding, Lukasz Szpruch, Yue Zhang

item.title: on\'ona: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
item.description: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce on\'ona, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate on\'ona across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, on\'ona lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.
item.dc:creator: Cheng Luo, Xinnan Dai, Zhongzhu Zhou, Zefan Cai, Ruijie Zhu, Tianyu Zhang, Junjie Hu

item.title: LongCapHarness: Capability-Guided Auto-Harnessing for Long-Context Reasoning
item.description: Existing methods enhancing an LLM's long-context reasoning capability often rely on data synthesis and follow-up LLM post-training. However, the data synthesis strategy and the post-training recipes are empirically driven and computationally intensive. In this work, we propose a new framework, dubbed LongCapHarness, to instead harness the underlying capabilities for long-context reasoning. The harnessing process recursively revises and updates capability primitive implementation, capability state and control logic through recursive self-improvement on the development set. With neither data synthesis nor LLM post-training, LongCapHarness is applied to Llama3-8B and transferred to Qwen2.5-3B. LongCapHarness substantially outperforms recent data-synthesis-based baselines on HELMET and RULER benchmarks; its estimated development cost is less than 50% of the estimated training costs of NExtLong and PolicyLong. We hope these results motivate further research into harnessing the latent capabilities of LLMs to solve tasks beyond their explicit training.
item.dc:creator: Tao Zhang, Yuhang He

item.title: ASCENT: Scale-Complementary External State for Frozen Long-Context Language Models
item.description: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is -15.88 points [-20.55, -11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B-8B readers obtain 66.75-85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.
item.dc:creator: Xingjian Zhang

item.title: Retrofitting Unbounded Context onto Stock Language Models
item.description: A language model that never had to forget would keep every document it has read and every turn it has spoken, and answer from any of it. This paper shows that two stock models can do that on unmodified weights by manipulating their geometry. Rotary attention turns each pair of key dimensions, a plane, at its own rate. The slow planes turn once in thousands of tokens and carry the address a query matches when it reads a far key; the fast planes turn once in a few tokens, and the order of the tokens inside a span is already written into its keys and values by the time the span leaves the near window. At distance the position blurs, and what attention reads is a bag rather than a sequence. A far span is read by its words: under competition it is read only if it is visible at the query of the question's own handle word, and a read through a description rather than a word fails at distance in every model measured, a 70B included. These facts allow a trick. What sits in the far part of attention does not have to be the history as it was; it can be installed ahead of the prediction. The design keeps a near window of 8K tokens at their true positions and changes what lies beyond it with the prompt: every far key and value goes to the host exact, a word index finds the units the request's rare words name, a far window of slots inside the trained range holds them while the request is encoded, and a rare word the model generates fetches its units mid-generation with one exact re-encode. Implemented in llama.cpp on Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, the design reads planted single needles at 99 to 100 of 100 and three-key discrimination at 88 to 100 of 100 from 32K to one million tokens, scores 70.8 on RULER against 69.9 for dense attention on Llama-3.1-8B at 128K and 67.8 against 75.5 on Mistral-7B at 32K, and at 128K prefills at 1.85 times and decodes at 1.65 to 1.68 times stock speed.
item.dc:creator: Mark Oskin

item.title: Programming Prescience: Issues in Human Construction of Forecasting Bots
item.description: AI models' growing capacity for complex reasoning has made them attractive tools for forecasting, or the systematic prediction of the future based on past and present data. However, should AI forecasting systems be adopted, human builders will shoulder the work of building and evaluating them. In this paper, we explore what this work looks like with a qualitative interview study with 15 builders of forecasting bots, sampled from among successful participants in a recent AI forecasting competition. Our analysis surfaces the challenges around (1) tuning a bot to acquire factual research, (2) implementing coherent reasoning, and (3) understanding how well one's bot actually does. During their work, builders frequently introduced complexity that did not pay off, and tested in ways that were opportunistic and piecemeal. Our detailed account of their challenges helps clarify what problems should be targeted in upcoming innovations in process, tools, and human-AI teaming for forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Priya Dhawka, Benjamin Wilson, Andrew Head

item.title: 2D Gum-Net: Unsupervised Dense Elastic Image Registration via Symmetric Correlation and Spectral Pooling
item.description: Dense non-rigid registration, the recovery of a pixel-wise deformation field that warps one image into geometric agreement with another, is fundamental across medical imaging, structural biology, and correspondence estimation, yet learning-based approaches face a severe bottleneck: ground-truth deformation fields are notoriously difficult to obtain for real data. We present 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised. We transfer the Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net), originally developed for 3D subtomogram alignment in cryo-electron tomography, to 2D elastic registration: all three modules are redesigned in 2D, and the rigid transformation head is replaced by a Dense Spatial Transformer that regresses a sparse control-point grid, lifted to a full-resolution field $\Phi$ by bicubic interpolation. Downsampling uses DCT spectral pooling, implemented as frozen-basis matrix multiplications ($\approx 50\times$ GPU speedup), preserving the fine, quasi-periodic structure that max and average pooling destroy. We evaluate on contact-based fingerprints, a challenging testbed for this task: locally self-similar ridge patterns make correspondence maximally ambiguous, skin pressed against a sensor generates authentic large-displacement elastic distortion, and minutiae act as precise landmarks through which an independent matcher externally verifies the topological correctness of predicted fields. Trained purely on synthetic impressions and evaluated zero-shot on real benchmarks, our method improves structural correlation by up to 15.7% on FVC2004 and raises genuine match scores under an independent matcher while leaving imposter scores essentially unchanged. This suggests that the predicted deformations restore true structure without fabricating correspondences.
item.dc:creator: Aarya Bhave, Anushka Ajay Bhave

item.title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce \textsc{NarrativeBench}, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. \textsc{NarrativeBench} provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.
item.dc:creator: Nikhil Sharma, Kelly Marchisio, Kenton Murray, Ziang Xiao

item.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
item.description: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is increasingly used to improve language model reasoning, yet its effects on sequential decision procedures remain poorly understood. We study this problem in clinical multi-turn agents that must decide what information to request, when to stop gathering evidence, and which action to take. We introduce three controlled environments: medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration, each with hidden clinical states, query costs, exact adaptive oracles, and deterministic outcome verifiers. Across these tasks, outcome-only group relative policy optimization often improves aggregate reward while producing undesirable procedures, including premature commitment, one-question collapse, and failures on rare high-risk cases. In diagnostics, assigning dense credit to questions that reduce uncertainty improves held-out value and moderate-case support across three training seeds relative to outcome-only reinforcement learning, without the high-risk seed collapse observed under outcome-only training. Separating exploration from exploitation further increases high-risk support at its best checkpoint, but at the cost of excessive information gathering on low-acuity cases. Additional experiments show that the optimal strength of process credit is task-dependent; that after a supervised warmup that already gathers carefully, reinforcement learning raises aggregate reward by trimming questions while degrading high-risk performance; and that reinforcement learning does not reliably repair rare behavior gaps inherited from biased supervised data. Verifiable final outcomes are therefore insufficient for training reliable multi-turn agents: reward design must account for the procedure used to reach an answer, and evaluation must distinguish adaptive information gathering from reward-exploiting shortcuts.
item.dc:creator: Brendan P. Murphy, Agustina Saenz

item.title: reComposer: Editable Planning for Controllable Image Generation
item.description: Prompt-based image generation makes it easy to produce visual assets, but offers little support for engaging with the creative process. Prompting collapses interdependent creative decisions into a monolithic instruction and returns a finished image, leaving control limited to revising the prompt or correcting the model's output. We present reComposer, a process-oriented image-generation interface built around editable planning, which decomposes users' evolving intent into meaningful creative decisions - such as subject, composition, or palette - and collaborates with users to explore underspecified goals and alternatives. reComposer supports conversational and direct manipulation of the plan, moving between concept-level intent and visual-level control. We evaluated reComposer with 8 design and non-design professionals. Compared to prompting, participants felt greater control and ownership while developing visual assets, exploring alternatives, and iterating on details. Our findings suggest how shifting generative AI interaction from specifying outputs to shaping process can support creative thinking alongside asset production.
item.dc:creator: Susie S. Y. Li, Angie Boggust, Fred Hohman, Donghao Ren, Dominik Moritz, Yannick Assogba

item.title: HumanSightBench: A Benchmark for Human Visual Perception in MLLMs
item.description: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on knowledge-intensive and reasoning-based vision-language benchmark datasets, but still struggle to solve the visual questions that people can solve easily. Evaluating the differences between MLLMs and human-level visual perception is challenging due to end-to-end evaluation which combines various skills, or because we are uncertain if individual items are valid. Specifically, observed errors may reflect visual perception, language priors, background knowledge, question ambiguity, and underspecified answers. Our guideline for HumanSightBench is that we construct items that are human-easy by construction and model-hard by evaluation. HumanSightBench contains 2,876 visual questions with short answers across 7 top-level perceptual categories and 21 subcategories. We only include items that pass five inclusion gates: question clarity, answer uniqueness, visual grounding, human solvability, and text-only shortcut filtering. According to the protocol, errors are defined as incorrect answers on human-validated visual tasks with the evaluated interface. The inclusion gates are intended to reduce confounds from ambiguity and external knowledge. The best pass@3 score is 65.6% across eight evaluated MLLMs. No evaluated model exceeds 27.5% on Counting. These results identify capability gaps that are hidden by overall scores and can help future training experiments and held-out evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Zixin Su, Yangguang Lin, Zegang Peng, Yuntong Sun, Xuanyi Wang, Jiahao Wang, Qiankai Xu, Bing Yuan, Jinze Bai, Youbin Wu, Jingjia Huang, Ruyang Liu, Yanxu Hu

item.title: TS-GEAR: Taobao Shangou GEnerative Ad Retrieval
item.description: On-demand delivery platforms such as DoorDash and Uber Eats impose a constraint absent in traditional e-commerce: merchants beyond the user's delivery range are invalid candidates rather than merely low-ranked. Generative retrieval has recently shown strong potential in large-scale retrieval systems. Adapting it to this setting, however, poses three challenges. First, existing semantic IDs encode geography only as a soft signal, so reachability can only rely on a non-differentiable post-generation hard truncation. Second, user preferences vary substantially across both regions and queries, so aggregating historical behaviors without conditioning on geography and the current query yields biased interest estimates. Third, the retrieved candidate set is evaluated by its collective value, yet autoregressive training scores each sequence independently, with no set-level signal to discourage redundant near-duplicates. To address the challenges, we propose TS-GEAR, a unified generative retrieval framework for on-demand delivery: (1) Geo-Semantic ID splits merchant identifiers into geographic prefixes and semantic suffixes, making reachability a prediction target rather than a post-hoc filter; (2) Query-Geo Target Attention aggregates historical behaviors using the real-time query and location as dual targets, while encoding each behavior's own location into its attention key; (3) GMPO (Group Marginal Policy Optimization) rewrites advantages using a deduplicated group reward and marginal advantage within GRPO, avoiding auxiliary diversity objectives. Deployed online with a lightweight 0.1B backbone, TS-GEAR serves over 150 million queries per day in the search advertising pipeline of Taobao Shangou, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on both HitRate and geographic validity, and achieving 3.8% gains in ad impressions and 4.2% in ad revenue.
item.dc:creator: Guofeng Tong, Xu Zhang, Guangliang Yu, Haiqiang Wang, Guannan Cong, Xing Guo, Yang Zhou, Jingjing Duan, Shuang Li, Feng Shi, Hualei Liu

item.title: Embodied First Exam
item.description: Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential paradigm shift toward using coding agents to control robots. Existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning, leaving it open whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints. We therefore introduce the Embodied First Exam, a unified, comprehensive, and agent-native evaluation framework where coding agents can choose their own control approach: direct control, code to control, or train a policy to control. We hope it serves as a first exam for coding agents before they enter the physical world, with 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, including 9 new suites that go beyond pick-and-place to spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control, and sim-to-sim engineering. Each task can be run in up to three evaluation settings. The Standard Setting mimics the real world: the agent receives only sensor observations and, by default, cannot reset the environment. Its Realtime variant keeps the environment running while the agent reasons. The Privileged Setting gives the agent access to the full simulator state and unlimited resets, allowing it to search for an oracle solution for training purposes. Success rates in this setting serve as an approximate upper bound. On the 456 core tasks, the strongest of eight agents, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, achieves a success rate of 34% in the Standard Setting, leaving much room for improvement. To see where agents fail, we label the stage at which failed attempts go wrong and compare failures across agents, settings, and stage categories.
item.dc:creator: Kangrui Wang, Qineng Wang, Changhe Chen, Pingyue Zhang, Chi Gui, Feishi Wang, Canyu Chen, Wenli Xiao, Xiaoyu Huang, Tonghe Zhang, Linjie Li, Zihan Wang, Minyeong Kim, Yiyou Sun, Mingkai Deng, Jinyu Hou, Qi Zhu, Han Liu, Eric P. Xing, Huaxiu Yao, Zhiwen Fan, Yuejiang Liu, Dawn Song, Pieter Abbeel, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Yuke Zhu, Guanya Shi, Ruohan Zhang, Manling Li

item.title: Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization
item.description: Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior closed-book. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier for self-distillation.
item.dc:creator: Shayan Talaei, Agam Bhatia, Arshia Soltani Moakhar, Jonas H\"ubotter, Amin Saberi, Azalia Mirhoseini

item.title: MixRoute: Rethinking Single-Distribution Training for Generalizable Neural Routing
item.description: Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) is a promising paradigm for solving routing problems, yet its generalization across diverse data distributions remains a critical bottleneck. Existing methods typically tackle cross-distribution generalization through complex multi-distribution training or intricate meta-learning schemes, implicitly presuming that single-distribution training yields a weak zero-shot baseline. In this paper, we demonstrate that the potential of single-distribution training has been substantially underestimated and can be unlocked by a simple architectural inductive bias: Mix Normalization. To approach this, we first construct a comprehensive benchmark spanning three representative routing problems and 179 fine-grained datasets, capturing diverse shifts in node coordinates, customer demands, capacity and time windows. Building on this benchmark, we propose MixRoute, a neural framework that adaptively combines normalization statistics at different granularities to mitigate varying distribution shifts. Trained exclusively on uniform distributions, MixRoute generalizes effectively to a wide range of unseen distributions without any distribution-specific adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MixRoute consistently achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot generalization. Our work revisits normalization as a parsimonious alternative for zero-shot generalization against complex training-adaptation schemes.
item.dc:creator: Hang Yi, Ziwei Huang, Yining Ma, Zhiguang Cao

item.title: Shaping Useful Noise: Energy Distributions Predict Visual Pretraining Quality
item.description: Synthetic data can scale visual pretraining, but current selection criteria only partially explain which datasets train strong representations. We propose using the energy profile of a dataset--the distribution of log-probability levels it occupies under a normalised real-image density model--as an audit and curation principle for synthetic data. To operationalise this view, we introduce Energy-Level Distribution Distance (ELD), which compares real and synthetic energy distributions. Real images span sparse high-likelihood scenes and dense low-likelihood textures, so useful synthetic data should cover this energy range rather than collapse to likely but low-variation samples. Across diverse synthetic datasets, ELD exposes mismatches missed by FID and predicts pretraining performance beyond FID, LPIPS variation, and feature-space recall, including across CNN and ViT self-supervised settings. We then use ELD to resample and mix synthetic sources, matching the real-image energy histogram while preserving diversity and improving downstream transfer.
item.dc:creator: Ching Lam Choi, Antonio Torralba, Phillip Isola, Stefanie Jegelka

item.title: Attention Is Only as Good as Its Witnesses: When Higher-Order Layers Help, and When They Do Not
item.description: Transformers stop learning graph search as graphs grow, and learn the card game SET only after many distinct questions, although attention can represent both. We read these failures, and the uneven record of higher-order attention, from what a layer sums over: each layer we study computes the partition function of a family of witnesses and reads it at a temperature. Two laws follow. The depth law is a known result of logic, which we state for these layers: L layers over two-step walks reach exactly 2^L - 1 steps, just as a logical statement with L nested clauses of the form "there is a vertex such that" sees exactly that far. We build a construction that reaches this far, checked in Lean, and, when vertices carry no names, no such network reaches further. The size law is the cost of reading at a temperature, which logic does not have: existence is read correctly at every size, in the worst case, if and only if inverse temperature times margin is at least the logarithm of the number of candidates. Layers built on these laws, and on two principles that we test, learn where Transformers fail. One propagator layer trained on 49-vertex graphs answers every question at every search depth on 250-vertex graphs. Given the modulus 3, exponential Newton computes the softmax of 2-simplicial attention over pairs exactly in 3^d n operations for d clocks; with six clocks it learns SET from as few deals as 2-simplicial attention and transfers from 8- to 20-card tables. On CLRS-30 without hints, a 186,000-parameter block of OR-join and power-mean channels matches (within half a point) or beats a model of at least 73 million parameters on 9 of 12 graph tasks of the official test set, and on 8 of 12 with freshly drawn test graphs. The same account explains where pair layers did not help and where parallel layers must loop.
item.dc:creator: Mostafa 'Neo' Mohsenvand

item.title: Late but Valuable: Why Deadlines Change the Measured Value of LLM Reasoning
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly plan and run experiments in automated laboratories. These experiments keep running while the model reasons and run on schedules with hard deadlines. If an LLM-generated answer arrives late, the system executes a safe fallback action instead, such as rejecting a sample. This creates a systems problem that standard serving metrics do not capture. An answer that matches the fallback adds no value, and answers that differ from the fallback may require more reasoning time. Reporting answer quality and latency separately can therefore overstate the value of reasoning. We test this on synthetic sample decisions, where the best choice is known exactly and a runtime enforces the deadline. We compare one LLM's fast mode, which answers directly, with its thinking mode, which reasons first. In a prespecified replay of 1,200 new decisions, thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones. Multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value that thinking delivered. This prediction overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision, and by 0.0191 in a repeat on 300 new decisions. Both 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. In a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment using simultaneous request bursts, raising the number of requests from 8 to 56 reduced the share of thinking answers that met a 45 s deadline from 79.2% to 1.4%, although total output tripled. Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should therefore measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.
item.dc:creator: Sina Barazandeh, Benjamin E. Lundell, Jose Lugo-Martinez

item.title: Publications as benchmarks: auditing AI agents on spatial transcriptomics alignment
item.description: AI agents are increasingly automating data analysis, but responsible adoption requires reliable performance evaluation, which is costly in specialized scientific domains. We introduce a framework that translates scientific publications into auditable benchmarks for AI agents and demonstrate its use on spatial transcriptomics alignment tasks. Across 121 tasks, 16 baseline methods, and six AI agents, the best agents (GPT-6-Astra and Gemini-4-Argon) matched or outperformed all baselines on 80% of tasks, often using surprisingly simple heuristics. Agent performance was robust to prompting and access to pre-installed packages. Benchmark construction also uncovered errors in prior work and shortcuts in current evaluation metrics. Finally, we show that agent-generated solutions can be distilled into a reusable program that ranks in the top 10% of baseline methods on unseen data. Our framework offers a scalable way to evaluate AI agents in specialized scientific domains by leveraging and stress-testing existing papers and metrics.
item.dc:creator: Yiqun T. Chen, Jan Matthias, Jianing Yao, Hongyu Eric Zhao, Stephanie C. Hicks

item.title: ShadowBench-MCP: Measuring Shadow Invocations in MCP-Style Tool Routing
item.description: LLM agents increasingly act as routers for tools, APIs, and software-supply-chain workflows, making an execution path - rather than generated text alone - a security-relevant model output. We study shadow invocation: a task-preserving request variant that causes an LLM router to select a riskier execution path, potentially skipping validation, provenance, staging, redaction, or audit controls even though the request does not ask for a malicious action. We introduce ShadowBench-MCP, a benchmark and metric suite that separates task preservation (TPSS), operational pressure (OPSS), and route-geometric drift (RGAS), and combines them in the pre-execution SODS score. In a focused policy-ablation study using a Groq-hosted qwen/qwen3-32b router, 120 routing decisions yield 96 original-versus-variant comparisons across six security-sensitive workflows. Efficiency-first routing produces a 29.2% shadow-invocation rate and 26.7% safety-tool skip rate. Policy-aware routing reduces these to 4.2% and 1.7%, respectively, corresponding to an 85.7% relative reduction in shadow invocations. Pre-execution signals distinguish shadow routes with ROC AUC up to 0.94. These results are early, single-router evidence of a policy-dependent routing-layer security effect, not a claim of universal vulnerability.
item.dc:creator: Eyhab Al-Masri, Wenjun Yang

item.title: LocateAnyMesh: Grounding 3D Mesh Queries in 2D Images with Vision-Language Models
item.description: Textured 3D meshes specify object geometry and appearance, making them a natural query for finding a particular asset in an image. We introduce LocateAnyMesh, a vision-language model that uses the mesh itself as part of its prompt. A frozen 3D encoder maps colored surface points to a compact token sequence, which a learned connector places alongside image and instruction tokens. We evaluate two grounding models with PPAT mesh tokens: LAM-Select selects image-region proposals, while LAM-Direct predicts coordinates directly. Neither requires rendered query views or view-template matching. New objects require a single encoder pass and no object-specific fine-tuning. LAM-Select improves localization on the reported real-image suites and the official BOP YCB-V evaluation. Secondary experiments compare mesh encoders, and a LAM-Direct study isolates surface color. A single-seed LAM-Select continuation supplies pointing and mesh-only description evidence without replacing the reported localization model. The results support mesh tokens as a query representation, with remaining limitations in presence decisions, identity binding, proposal coverage, and descriptive fidelity.
item.dc:creator: Chris Choy, Zhiding Yu, Jan Kautz

item.title: Perturbing Inputs Improves Pretraining Distillation
item.description: Knowledge distillation trains a student language model to match a teacher's predictions on the training text. We ask whether learning the teacher's behavior beyond the training text can further improve the student. We investigate this using three input perturbations: additive token noise, blending two documents, and blending neighboring tokens. Specifically, for an early part of pretraining we perturb the inputs and train the student to match the teacher on them, and we spend the rest of the same token budget on ordinary distillation. When pretraining from scratch, the best method improves on standard distillation at both scales we tried, by 0.025 nats at 135M parameters and by 0.020 nats at 0.5B (mean of three seeds). At 135M this is 1.45 times the gain that distillation itself provides over next-token training. We also observe promising downstream transfer: at 0.5B, the best variant improves average zero-shot accuracy by about one percentage point across seven tasks. It also retains its validation-loss advantage after low-bit weight quantization. We also test a data-limited setting in which training data must be reused, and find that the gains persist. Finally, ablations suggest that, for additive noise, perturbing the teacher's inputs contributes most of the gain, while perturbing only the student's inputs yields much less.
item.dc:creator: Ziyang Cai, Yihe Dong, Dimitris Papailiopoulos, Shivam Garg

item.title: When Should Diffusion Language Models Reconsider Their Commitments?
item.description: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) are well known for fast text generation via parallel decoding. However, independent parallel sampling can commit to inconsistent predictions, and less is known about how to selectively revise these early token commitments. In this work, we introduce $\underline{\mathrm{P}}$lanned $\underline{\mathrm{U}}$nmasking-and-$\underline{\mathrm{R}}$evision Joint $\underline{\mathrm{L}}$earning (PURL) for MDMs, a training-based framework that seamlessly unifies parallel generation with selective token revision. We derive a normalized joint transition whose likelihood factorizes into edit selection, unmask selection, and token prediction. These components are trained jointly on partially masked sequences constructed according to the model's own unmasking policy. During inference, all three decisions are supported by a single shared forward pass, enabling the model to decode masked tokens and revise noisy tokens. Across logic puzzles, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, PURL improves accuracy at matched unmask budgets, with relative gains up to 47.4% accuracy improvement and up to an $8\times$ reduction in scheduled decoding rounds. Beyond these gains, our analysis further reveals general principles of revisable decoding: token edits become more effective as context accumulates; early edits can steer unfinished trajectories, whereas later edits tend to remain localized; and effective edits therefore depend on both calibrating when to intervene and learning where and how to revise. Together, these suggest that effective parallel generation depends not on revising more tokens, but on making the right commitments revisable at the right time.
item.dc:creator: Haoyang Zheng, Yidong Ouyang, Blake Jianhang Chen, Tian Tan, Ziqian Lin, Liqian Peng, Alec Go, Guang Lin

item.title: K-PWM: Control-Oriented Structured Bilinear World Models under Partial Observation
item.description: World models learn internal simulators of environment dynamics for prediction, planning, and control, yet learning them from limited, noisy, and partial observations remains challenging. While much progress has focused on pixel-based observations, many physical systems instead provide vector-valued measurements that reveal only part of the underlying state. We introduce K-PWM, a probabilistic world model for prediction and control under partial observation. K-PWM couples Koopman-bilinear latent dynamics with a nonlinear observation decoder and performs probabilistic latent-state inference through the learned model via extended Kalman filtering and smoothing, without a separately trained inference network. Its bilinear structure enables exact propagation of the maintained Gaussian belief through the latent transition and efficient rollouts for uncertainty-aware model predictive path integral (MPPI) control. For training K-PWM, we present a generalized expectation conditional maximization (GECM) procedure with closed-form updates for the generators, noise covariances, and latent prior, complemented by gradient-based decoder learning. A Koopman-consistent initialization selects the latent dimension from data and initializes the action-dependent dynamics. With limited training data, K-PWM achieves lower long-horizon prediction error than the evaluated baselines on partially observed Gymnasium MuJoCo systems, while substantially reducing training time relative to the strongest prediction baseline. On high-dimensional MuJoCo Menagerie robots, it achieves competitive tracking accuracy with low per-step computation times, demonstrating potential for real-time deployment. These results support structured probabilistic dynamics as a data- and compute-efficient approach to world modeling and control under partial observation.
item.dc:creator: Santosh Mohan Rajkumar, Sriram Narayanan, Samuel E. Otto, Debdipta Goswami

item.title: MOMENT-DP: Momentum Aware Evaluation of Correlated Noise for Differentially Private Training
