item.description: Temporally correlated noise can substantially improve the utility of differentially private optimization, yet candidate mechanisms are commonly designed or evaluated using only partial information about the optimization process, such as workload structure, learning-rate schedules, or local curvature. We study whether persistent optimizer state provides additional information that can change the relative utility of privacy-valid correlated-noise mechanisms. We introduce MOMENT-DP, an optimizer-state-aware framework that models how temporally correlated privacy noise propagates through momentum-based optimization. For locally quadratic objectives, MOMENT-DP expresses privacy-induced final loss through an optimizer transfer operator that jointly captures curvature, learning-rate scheduling, momentum, and temporal noise covariance. NoiseCurve's curvature-aware quadratic criterion is recovered exactly as the zero-momentum, constant-learning-rate special case. Changing only momentum while holding curvature, schedule, privacy calibration, and candidate mechanisms fixed induces genuine mechanism-ranking reversals. The effect persists outside exact quadratic dynamics in per-example-clipped private logistic regression, while remaining unresolved in the neural regime we study. These results establish optimizer state as an under-modeled, decision-relevant axis in evaluating temporally correlated privacy noise.
item.dc:creator: Sunny Gupta, Raja Viswanadha

item.title: Does Predictive Performance Translate to Causal Performance? Evaluating tabular foundation models as nuisance learners for causal effect estimation
item.description: Tabular foundation models based on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) achieve strong predictive performance, but their value for causal inference is unclear. We evaluated whether PFNs, which predict through in-context learning, could match or outperform conventional nuisance learners in supporting accurate causal estimation and reliable uncertainty quantification (inference). Learners modeled propensity scores and outcome regressions within doubly robust estimators of average causal effects, with and without cross-fitting, across synthetic and semi-synthetic settings with varying confounding complexity and effect heterogeneity. Under simple parametric data-generating processes, the PFNs were competitive with correctly specified parametric regressions and ensembles containing them. In more complex settings, they outperformed all conventional learners evaluated, including richly specified Super Learner ensembles, for both accuracy and uncertainty quantification. As sample size increased, only the two PFN models (TabPFN and Mitra) consistently approached nominal confidence interval coverage, whereas under-coverage persisted for conventional learners. In some settings, PFNs achieved near-nominal coverage and well-calibrated standard errors even without cross-fitting. At the smallest sample size (n=200) and in the higher-dimensional semi-synthetic settings, PFNs and other flexible learners exhibited poor coverage without cross-fitting. For PFNs, this appeared to be driven by propensity score overfitting consistent with in-sample memorization of treatment labels. These findings highlight the promise of prior-data fitted networks as in-context nuisance learners for causal estimation, while underscoring the need for further evaluation in challenging settings.
item.dc:creator: Andrew R Weckstein, Issa J Dahabreh, Marinka Zitnik, Sonia Hern\'andez-D\'iaz, Sebastian Schneeweiss

item.title: SGA-Sparse: Training Native SwiGLU Gates for Activation-Sparse and Low-Bit LLMs
item.description: Activation sparsity can reduce FFN weight traffic during single-user LLM decoding, but active channels must be identified early enough to avoid fetching unused weights. In pretrained SwiGLU models, training-free routing with the native gate performs substantially worse than routing with the up activation at high sparsity. We show that this ordering reverses after sparsity-aware training. Based on this insight, we introduce SGA-Sparse, which converts pretrained SwiGLU LLMs into fixed-budget activation-sparse models by training the existing gate projection directly as a top-k router. SGA-Sparse updates all model parameters end-to-end while preserving the original SwiGLU activation and introducing no auxiliary router parameters. After approximately 30B training tokens, LLaMA models from 1B to 8B achieve uniform per-token 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while remaining within 0.2-2.7 pp of their original dense checkpoints in average zero-shot accuracy. Because post-training quantization degrades sparsity-trained checkpoints, we further study two complementary quantization-aware training (QAT) recipes: continued-QAT largely recovers performance at 4-bit weight quantization, while joint-QAT performs better for the more aggressive sub-4-bit target. To compare activation sparsity with dense low-bit quantization, we translate the sparsity-induced reduction in weight traffic into an equivalent bit-width. Under this unified weight-traffic metric, our 2.5- and 1.5-bit-equivalent models establish a new accuracy-traffic Pareto frontier: the 2.5-bit-equivalent models match dense 3-bit QAT accuracy, while the 1.5-bit-equivalent models approach dense 2-bit models and outperform dense ternary models by 1.3 pp on average. These results establish native-gate training as a practical approach for combining high FFN sparsity with low-bit weights.
item.dc:creator: Ruokai Yin, Steven Li

item.title: Not Yet in the Profile: Uncertainty-Aware Dynamic User Profiling by Learning from Future Interactions
item.description: On the Web, user profiling builds compact user representations from interaction histories for efficient personalization, and dynamic user profiling updates them as users' behavior and preferences change. However, new user behavior can be ambiguous, and its interpretation differs across users. To address this, we introduce Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Profile Manager (UAPM), which separates the claims in a user profile from interpretations of new behavior that are not yet confirmed, through a Profile, a Buffer, and a Rulebook. UAPM records user-specific interpretation and update rules in the Rulebook, keeps ambiguous evidence in the Buffer outside the Profile as evidence for later decisions, and writes supported general and situational characteristics to the Profile. We train UAPM with Privileged On-Policy Distillation with Dual Specialization (POPD-DS), which learns from recorded future interactions during training without access to them at deployment. Its first stage, Dual Specialization, distills a stronger model into a current-only Student and a future-informed model that becomes the Teacher. In the second stage, privileged on-policy distillation (POPD), only the fixed Teacher receives future interactions and guides the Student's own management decisions alongside task rewards. Experiments on three Web personalization tasks show that UAPM outperforms multiple baselines under the same downstream input budget, improving on the best same-budget baseline by up to 5%.
item.dc:creator: Jieyong Kim, Neil Shah, Dong Wang

item.title: DISCOVER: Online Variance-Guided Data Discovery for Budgeted Multimodal GRPO
item.description: Recent advances in reinforcement learning have made verifiable rewards a central post-training paradigm for improving multimodal reasoning. However, methods such as GRPO remain data- and compute-inefficient, spending rollout and annotation budget on prompts that provide little learning signal. We propose DISCOVER, an online data-discovery framework for budgeted multimodal GRPO that enables vision-language models to dynamically identify prompts that are most useful for the current policy. DISCOVER first organizes the multimodal sample pool into semantic clusters and queries a small set of density-diverse representative samples to obtain initial reward observations. During training, it estimates the utility of unannotated samples by transferring sparse reward feedback from queried samples. Since sample utility changes as the policy evolves, DISCOVER dynamically updates these estimates with recency-weighted rollout observations. It then selects only high-utility prompts for annotation using a policy-conditioned score that accounts for reward variance and difficulty. Once the discovery budget is exhausted, DISCOVER continues with utility-based replay. Experiments on ViRL39K and VLAA-Thinking with Qwen3-VL-2B show that DISCOVER substantially improves multimodal mathematical reasoning under a strict 10% unique-sample budget, outperforming budget-matched random selection, hard-example sampling, full-pool GRPO under the same training-step budget, and online selection baselines. Ablations further validate the importance of semantic coverage, online reward transfer, and stable discovery cadence, establishing DISCOVER as a practical framework for data-efficient multimodal RL post-training.
item.dc:creator: Peyman Gholami, Shivam Chandhok, Saber Malekmohammadi, Shayan Shams, Robert Xiao, Leonid Sigal

item.title: System Prompts Affect Response Bias More Than Discriminability in LLM Safety
item.description: Large language model safety evaluations often focus on a compliance-refusal tradeoff: models should refuse unsafe requests without refusing safe ones. We argue that this misses a broader form of prompt-conditioned task selection, where the same request can elicit different behaviors depending on the system prompt. We investigate this using a controlled evaluation crossing eight safety-task prompt families with three clarity levels across HarmBench, XSTest, and IHEval. Holding benchmark items fixed, we evaluate 13 models and use signal detection theory to distinguish two possibilities: whether models become better at telling safe from unsafe requests (discriminability), or simply more willing to refuse (response criterion). We find substantial differences in discriminability across models, but system prompts primarily shift the willingness to refuse, with smaller and less consistent effects on discriminability. Increasing prompt clarity makes models more willing to refuse without reliably improving their ability to distinguish safe from unsafe requests. Beyond refusal, prompt families also shift responses among six distinct behavioral policies, including clarification and safe help. Together, these findings show that system prompts primarily change how models respond to safety-relevant requests rather than consistently improving their ability to distinguish safe from unsafe ones.
item.dc:creator: Mohan W. Gupta, Sandy Tanwisuth

item.title: Target Recoverability under Selective Labels: A Failure Mode in ECG-Based Acute Coronary Syndrome Prediction
item.description: Medical machine learning models often learn from diagnoses observed only in patients clinicians chose to test. The biases of such selective labels are well known, but less understood is what happens when a diagnosis includes cases the model's inputs cannot detect. Because testing decisions draw on information the model does not see, these cases can appear predictable among tested patients, producing relationships that fail, and can even reverse, among the untested. We formalize this mechanism and show in simulations that it worsens as testing becomes more selective or undetectable cases more common, while models trained only on detectable cases remain informative. We empirically study electrocardiogram (ECG)-based prediction of acute coronary syndrome (ACS), which is confirmed only by invasive testing and whose subtypes differ in how clearly they appear on the ECG. Three ECG foundation models fine-tuned on revascularization, our ACS proxy, performed well among catheterized patients (AUROC 0.740-0.770) but worse than chance for 30-day major adverse cardiovascular events among untested patients (AUROC 0.381-0.478). Models trained on ECG-visible subtypes retained discrimination (AUROC 0.680-0.709), whereas a model trained on unstable angina, which can occur without ECG changes, was inversely related to risk (AUROC 0.310). Under selective labels, effective learning therefore requires prediction targets that can be inferred from the model's inputs and evaluation in the intended deployment population, which often extends beyond the patients who were tested.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Schubert, Anton H{\aa}kansson, Ziad Obermeyer

item.title: Finite-Sample and Communication-Efficient Networked Information Aggregation
item.description: Building on SODA 2026 work Kearns et al. (2026), we study learning in directed acyclic graphs in which each agent observes only a subset of the input coordinates and may use the predictions of its parents as additional features. In the finite-sample protocol, the message sent along each edge is the agent's prediction vector on a shared sample, so the communication cost is linear in the sample size $m$. In this paper we study this model under communication constraints. First, we revisit the finite-sample analysis of the full-message protocol. We identify a gap in the finite-sample proof of Kearns et al. (2026) and develop a different argument that establishes a finite-sample population-risk guarantee along paths satisfying deterministic $M$-coverage. Second, we introduce a shared-sketch protocol in which each agent sends a $k$-dimensional linear sketch of its prediction vector instead of the full $m$-dimensional message, where $k\ll m$. We analyze this protocol through a reduction to least squares on the compressed sample together with an oblivious subspace embedding argument. The resulting bound separates statistics from communication: the statistical term is still governed by the original sample size $m$, while the additional error due to compression is controlled by the sketch dimension $k$. For Gaussian sketches, we obtain an explicit high-probability population-risk bound, showing that row subsampling is not the only possible communication-statistics tradeoff for networked information aggregation.
item.dc:creator: Mohammadhossein Bateni, Zahra Hadizadeh, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, Mahdi JafariRaviz, Shayan Taherijam

item.title: Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning
item.description: Learning accurate off-policy state-action value functions (Q-functions) from offline datasets becomes harder as the task horizon grows. One-step temporal-difference (TD) learning bootstraps after every transition, so small per-step errors accumulate along the horizon, and early states can be badly misvalued even when the TD loss is small. Multi-step TD shortens this chain by following the dataset trajectory for several steps; however, since the behavior policy is often suboptimal, every followed action adds a bias, and no fixed number of steps suits a whole trajectory. In this paper, we propose Horizon-Scalable Q-Learning (HQL), a simple method that enables accurate long-horizon value learning by automatically balancing between one-step and multi-step returns. HQL extends a target through a dataset action only when the critic values it at least as highly as the best-of-N actions sampled from the BC policy, and otherwise falls back to a one-step target. We show that this rule is a principled off-policy correction that needs no action densities, which makes HQL compatible with expressive flow and diffusion policies. Experiments show that HQL avoids the failures of both one-step and multi-step TD on a combination-lock task across horizons, and outperforms prior horizon-reduction methods on long-horizon OGBench and OCBench tasks.
item.dc:creator: Haoran Xu, Pragya Srivastava, Xinjie Liu, Siddhant Agarwal, Amy Zhang

item.title: Anatomy-Activated Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Pre-training
item.description: Medical Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) leverages the semantic richness of radiology reports to learn 3D representations, yet current architectures remain fundamentally anatomy-agnostic. While clinical diagnostics rely on organ-specific context, standard encoders apply a uniform, dense parameterization to all volumetric patches, and existing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers gate on isolated local features without explicit access to the organ composition of the scan or crop. We propose Anatomy-Activated Mixture-of-Experts (A$^{2}$MoE), a framework that incorporates anatomical inductive biases within the model's computational path. A$^{2}$MoE introduces two key components: (1) a Histogram Representation Router (HRR) that conditions expert selection on global visual context and a predicted anatomical composition histogram, encouraging anatomy-dependent expert weighting; and (2) an Organ-Query Multi-Scale Projector (OQMSP) that utilizes learnable queries to extract organ-level embeddings for fine-grained alignment without requiring manual annotations at inference. By routing at the patch level rather than the token level, A$^{2}$MoE reduces routing complexity by orders of magnitude while satisfying load balancing by construction. Pre-trained on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, A$^{2}$MoE achieves state-of-the-art performance across segmentation, classification, and detection benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our anatomically grounded inductive biases support robust generalization to MRI and ultrasound, establishing a scalable foundation for medical representation learning. The code is available at https://github.com/gmum/A2MoE.
item.dc:creator: Szymon P{\l}otka, Gizem Mert, Pedro R. A. S. Bassi, Wenxuan Li, Zongwei Zhou, Anna Marcinkiewicz, Wiktoria Roma\'nczyk, Jaros{\l}aw B. \'Cwik{\l}a, {\L}ukasz Struski, Ewa Szczurek, Jacek Tabor, Arkadiusz Sitek

item.title: CoupledFlow: One-Step Neural Operators for Coupled Multi-Physics PDEs
item.description: This paper introduces COUPLED FLOW, a new neural operator learning framework for multi-physics PDE systems that captures the co-evolution of multiple physical processes by modeling their cross-process interactions. Unlike existing neural operator methods that primarily target single-physics settings, COUPLED FLOW employs a novel structure-constrained flow matching algorithm to learn process- specific mean velocity fields conditioned on the full multi-physics state. This enables fast and accurate one-step prediction of coupled PDE systems that would otherwise require expensive numerical simulations. A key challenge in training COUPLED FLOW however lies in sampling structure-constrained conditional flow interpolants that capture cross-process correlations and serve as training examples for flow matching. To address this challenge, we derive a multi-physics mean-flow consistency identity that characterizes cross-process interactions and defines the structure-constrained mean-flow matching loss. To provide informative training samples for flow matching with this loss, we develop a principled method for sampling correlated conditional interpolants based on posterior multi-output Gaus- sian processes, which capture richer cross-process correlations than the commonly used endpoint-conditioned linear interpolants. We also establish a theoretical re- sult showing that the Wasserstein-2 distance between the predicted and oracle PDE solution distributions is upper-bounded in terms of the structure-constrained flow matching loss and the smoothness of the learned flow. Experiments across diverse coupled PDE benchmarks demonstrate that COUPLED FLOW consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art neural operators and generative PDE solvers.
item.dc:creator: Trong Khiem Tran, Minh Long Bui, Phi Le Nguyen, Mrinal Sen, Sanjay Srinivasan, Trong Nghia Hoang, Jana Doppa

item.title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
item.description: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Drishti Goel, Ethan M. Nguyen, Violeta J. Rodriguez, Koustuv Saha

item.title: Trained, Frozen, or Absent: Identifying What a Quantum Layer Contributes to Cross-Sectional Equity Ranking
item.description: Hybrid quantumclassical models are increasingly proposed for nancial prediction, but reported gains are rarely separated from the classical components around them. We study a hybrid quantum temporal convolutional network for daily cross-sectional ranking of 2000 Tokyo Stock Exchange equities under a protocol built to make the quantum contribution identiable: six conditions (circuit trained, frozen or absent, a parameter-matched classical surrogate, and the circuit alone, trained or frozen) through one code path; four walk-forward folds with ve seeds; bootstrap intervals, Deated Sharpe Ratios, backtest-overtting probabilities and family-wise error control; ve classical baselines including a gradient-boosted tree; and a locked holdout. On 500 out-of-sample days two one-sided tests place the trained-versus-frozen dierence inside 0.03 annualised Sharpe (p = 0.0055, minimum detectable eect 0.02): the circuit is equivalent to a frozen one, not merely indistinguishable from it. With the circuit as the head's only input the two are equivalent inside 0.25; against the network with no circuit the design resolves only 0.50. No condition is distinguishable from zero (best De-ated Sharpe Ratio 0.17). The holdout reproduces the ablation on a protable window, and 2000 US equities reproduce it where every condition loses money.
item.dc:creator: Chi-Sheng Chen, Xinyu Zhang, En-Jui Kuo, Rong Fu, Qiuzhe Xie, Fan Zhang

item.title: Adapting Large Language Models via Multi-Task Learning for Mental Health Problem, Emotion, and Sentiment Detection
item.description: This study investigates sequential multi-task learning using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), LoRA, and 4-bit quantization on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct for mental health problem detection, emotion detection, and sentiment analysis. Using 4,243 English social media posts, it compares two task sequences and demonstrates that task ordering significantly affects knowledge transfer and task interference. The MHP-first sequence achieves the best mental health problem detection (Micro-F1: 0.7624), while the Emotion-first sequence performs better in emotion (F1: 0.6052) and sentiment analysis (F1: 0.9459). A Joint-MTL baseline further highlights the challenges of simultaneous learning, including task interference and generative format collapse. Overall, the findings demonstrate the effectiveness of sequential PEFT for mental health NLP while showing that task order is critical to balancing performance across related tasks. The integration of LoRA and 4-bit quantization also reduces computational and memory requirements, supporting the adaptation of large language models in resource-constrained environments.
item.dc:creator: Amir Rafiq Bhat, Rahim Dehkharghani, Zeki Erdem

item.title: Who Remembers What? Multi-Granularity Memory Extraction for Multi-User, Multi-Agent Interaction
item.description: Self-evolving agents improve their own skills, memory, and harness code from experience without retraining the base LLM, and group-evolving agents go further by sharing these lessons across agents. Yet most such systems overlook that sharing across users and heterogeneous agents requires deciding who can benefit from each lesson and what information must remain private. We present MixUA, a memory system that distills independent user-agent trajectories into lessons and assigns each lesson to a user-agent pair, user, agent, or global scope according to whom it benefits and what it may disclose. For evaluation, we introduce CrossLearnBench, a mixed-user-agent benchmark that pairs established agent tasks with user preferences and privacy probes that test whether private facts leak into memory other users can read. With five users and seven agents, MixUA raises pass rates by up to 16 points over no memory and 5 over a single global memory, even on tasks previously tried only by other users on other agents. It retains up to 90% of previously stated preferences, and at most 0.02% of privacy probes find a planted private fact in a forbidden scope. We hope MixUA offers a scalable path toward a global system where users and agents co-evolve.
item.dc:creator: Yunzhe Wang, Mesut Erhan Unal, Sheng Zhang, Shabnam Ghadar, Peng Tang

item.title: Mental Imagery That Matters: Curing Latent Collapse in Multimodal Reasoning
item.description: Mental simulation, the ability to reason by constructing and updating internal visual states, is central to flexible human cognition, but remains elusive in current multimodal large language models. Latent multimodal reasoning offers a promising route toward this capability by interleaving text with continuous visual latent blocks, allowing models to maintain internal visual workspaces without decoding them into pixels. In this paper, we ask whether these latent visual states actually matter. Through a direct perturbation analysis across representative latent-reasoning MLLMs, we find that they often do not: dropping, replacing, or shuffling generated visual latents has only minor effects on the model's own final-answer probability, while equivalent perturbations to the linguistic reasoning trace are substantially more damaging. We call this failure mode Mental Simulation Collapse (MSC): the model appears to perform interleaved visual reasoning, but routes most answer-relevant computation through text. We further diagnose that MSC follows naturally from existing training objectives: visual alignment can make generated latents resemble helper-image embeddings, but it does not require the decoder to rely on them; subsequent text-only supervision further leaves the semantic role of the latent pathway unidentifiable. To address this, we introduce AnchorSim (Anchored Mental Simulation), a contrastive distillation framework that trains models to make their generated visual latents consequential. Across multiple visual reasoning benchmarks, AnchorSim improves performance, while diagnostic re-evaluation shows that visual perturbations now meaningfully affect predictions. Our results expose a fundamental failure mode of latent multimodal reasoning and demonstrate that mental simulation must be anchored to model behavior in order to matter.
item.dc:creator: Mi Luo, Rohan Dugad, Zihui Xue, Alex Dimakis, Kristen Grauman

item.title: Early Signals of Problematic AI Use: The Longitudinal Roles of Motivation and Emotional Engagement
item.description: Longitudinal evidence about the psychological impact of conversational AI use remains scarce. We report a survey study of 114 adults who reported their level of problematic AI use one year after reporting their motivations (for escape, social, entertainment, and instrumental reasons) for engaging with AI. We found high levels of AI motivation of all types predicted later problematic AI use, especially when participants turned to AI for managing their feelings and overcoming difficulties. Our findings imply that AI motivation could be used as an early warning signal of potential problematic use, especially if individuals engage with AI for emotional purposes over time.
item.dc:creator: Jina Suh, Constance Hadley, Koustuv Saha

item.title: Crustify: Repository-Level Generation of Safe Rust Bindings with LLM Agents and Coverage-Guided Testing
item.description: Wrapping C code in a safe Rust interface lets Rust applications use it without writing unsafe code, until the code itself is migrated to Rust. Such bindings are tedious and error-prone to write, however: their internals use unsafe code that the Rust compiler does not check, so a single mistake can introduce undefined behavior (UB), and they have so far been written mostly by hand. We present Crustify, an agentic co-translator that generates safe Rust bindings for repository-level C libraries. Crustify schedules a target's types and symbols into dependency-ordered waves of independent batches that agents bind concurrently. Its agents derive the ownership and lifecycle contract of every pointer and type they wrap, check each binding with coverage-guided equivalence and UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, and review every wave. They build on three tools that we contribute: (a) ffibox, Rust primitives for C/Rust interop that mirror Box, Arc, and Vec for C objects without ever forming a reference to memory that C may alias; (b) Wavefront, a neuro-symbolic static analyzer that orders a target's items by their dependencies, including those that casts and type-erased pointers hide; and (c) ffimap, a rustc-based analysis that maps the unsafe surface of bindings. On libgit2 and ffmpeg, with one developer in the loop, Crustify generated safe bindings for 41.9% and 42.8% of their public APIs in about 51.9 and 58.9 hours. On the interface consumers are expected to use, only 1.6% and 0.4% of the bindings' public functions are unsafe, and only 0.1% and 0.6% have a raw pointer in their signature. Their tests cover 98.92% and 99.07% of the Rust code and 45.95% and 67.20% of libgit2 and of ffmpeg's libavutil, and the reviewers fixed 8 and 13 defects that caused UB reachable from Rust. To our knowledge, this is the first work to automate the generation of safe Rust bindings for C libraries.
item.dc:creator: Marius Momeu, Marius Arvinte, Cory Cornelius, Koushik Sen

item.title: FEROM: Frontier Endogenous Reveal-Order Marginal Policy Optimization for Masked Diffusion LMs
item.description: Masked diffusion language models generate text by iteratively unmasking positions, with practical samplers often selecting reveal positions from the model's own logits. The reveal order is therefore an endogenous latent variable of the rollout process with an enormous discrete latent space. Policy optimization objectives relying on pre-defined schedules or sampled trajectories introduce either bias or high variance. In this paper, we propose FEROM, Frontier Endogenous Reveal-Order Marginal Policy Optimization, which approximates policy gradients for the rollout-induced marginal response policy of masked diffusion LMs. FEROM derives a Rao-Blackwellized policy-gradient identity over latent reveal orders and expresses the resulting estimator as posterior edge occupancy on a reveal-state DAG. To make marginalization practical, we introduce Frontier Reveal Marginalization, a budgeted estimator that approximates this marginal edge structure by combining CDF-based computation of local probabilities of the endogenous reveal process with frontier expansion of high-mass partial states. Integrated into a GRPO-style objective, FEROM replaces single-path log-scores with a detached token-score surrogate over posterior-relevant reveal edges. Experiments on math and coding tasks show comparable or improved results over existing methods under matched scoring-state budgets. An offline proxy study further shows improved marginal-gradient approximation with increased scoring budgets.
item.dc:creator: Zian Su, Ziyang Huang, Kaiyuan Zhang, Xiangyu Zhang

item.title: Transit-Oriented Land Use Planning Using Deep Reinforcement Learning
item.description: Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) is a key strategy for advancing sustainable urban development by promoting high-density, mixed-use land development within walking distance of public transit stations. However, traditional TOD planning often relies on heuristic methods, making it difficult to efficiently identify quantitatively optimized transit-oriented land use patterns. This paper presents DRL4TOD, a deep reinforcement learning framework that automatically optimizes land use types and floor area ratios (FARs) around transit stations in alignment with TOD principles. DRL4TOD incorporates a graph neural network to capture spatial interdependencies among land parcels, road networks, and metro stations, and uses a DRL-based optimization strategy to assign land-use types and FARs to selected parcels. It jointly optimizes multiple objectives, including land use density, land use diversity, and transit capacity utilization, while minimizing reconstruction costs to account for development feasibility. Applied to two real-world station areas in Shanghai, DRL4TOD consistently outperforms rule-based approaches and genetic algorithms, achieving more effective TOD outcomes with lower reconstruction costs. By adjusting objective weights, the framework enables flexible prioritization, such as placing greater emphasis on cost minimization when financial feasibility is a concern. These results demonstrate DRL4TOD's potential as a decision-support tool for generating coordinated land-use and FAR configurations under planner-specified priorities, rather than prescribing a single fixed design. For policymakers, the framework provides parcel-level, constraint-aware alternatives that make trade-offs among competing objectives explicit and support targeted decisions about development intensity and feasibility.
item.dc:creator: Bo Yang, Yuebing Liang, Zhan Zhao, Fangyi Ding, Yunhan Zheng, Shenhao Wang, Jinhua Zhao

item.title: VeV: Video-Enhanced Vibration Data Augmentation For Structural Difference
item.description: Surface-mounted vibration sensing provides non-invasive structural monitoring with high temporal fidelity across diverse ubiquitous computing scenarios such as smart farms, yet structure-borne wave models remain fragile to physical relocation and structural shifts. However, addressing this spatial data discontinuity remains limited by costly manual recalibration, insufficient physical grounding in data-driven synthesis, and substantial sim-to-real gaps in numerical digital twins. To resolve this spatial bottleneck without labor-intensive data recollection, we propose VeV, a physics-consistent spatial augmentation framework that synthesizes vibration responses at unmeasured target coordinates from sparse reference observations by coupling a monocular Vision-Derived Propagation Possibility Map for structural wave-guiding paths with a Visual Feature Map for transient source kinetics and implicit material dynamics. Evaluated on a 1,237 sensor-hour sow pig and piglet farm across disparate structures, VeV reduces waveform reconstruction MSE by over 57.5% compared to data-driven baselines and achieves up to 81.69% zero-shot classification accuracy, while reaching peak performance within just 30-50 calibration chunks to effectively eliminate cold-start retraining overhead and establish a scalable foundation extending to human-centric floor vibration sensing and ambient intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Joonhee Lee, Jiale Zhang, Sungmin Lee, Ruiqing Wang, Jeffrey Shulkin, Yiwen Dong, Pei Zhang, JeongGil Ko

item.title: RAD-TFM: Robust and Domain-Adapted Tabular Foundation Models
item.description: The development of tabular foundation models (TFMs) has accelerated in recent years, outperforming traditional ML methods on many tabular benchmarks. A key finding is that TFMs can be pretrained entirely on synthetic datasets, opening opportunities to design data generators that encourage desirable model properties. Prior work has mainly focused on crafting high-quality priors over generators to improve overall pretraining performance. Our key insight is that parameterizing the generator distribution enables an adversarial, distributional robustness perspective: during training, we can adapt the generator to emphasize datasets that are particularly challenging for the model, which we formalize by introducing an optimality gap measure. Further, we develop a method to align the synthetic data generation with real-world datasets from a given domain, constraining the adversary to generate realistic data. Together, these algorithms comprise the Robust and Domain-Adapted Tabular Foundation Models (RAD-TFM) pipeline, a model-agnostic adversarial training framework. Applied to the TabPFN V2 classifier, RAD-TFM improves performance across 6 diverse tabular benchmarks, with up to a 10.8 percentage-point improvement in mean normalized AUC over the strongest baseline, using fewer than 100k additional synthetic training datasets, less than 0.1% of the original pretraining data. Applying the same pipeline to TabICL V2 also improves performance across three major benchmarks, demonstrating the generality of the framework. These results highlight a promising new direction for targeted adversarial continued training of TFMs using synthetic data alone.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Peroni, Franck Le, Vadim Sheinin

item.title: GSynPEF: A Privacy Evaluation Framework for Synthetic Graphs
item.description: It is often desirable to generate and release synthetic graphs, which resemble real-world data, in a privacy-preserving way. While substantial progress has been made in designing private graph synthesizers (PGS), opportunities remain for more explicit connections between synthesizer models and privacy evaluation, and better accounting for output variation. This paper proposes GSynPEF, a practical framework for empirical evaluation of privacy and utility in settings for which a real-world graph is given as input and output synthetic graph(s) are observed. Our framework links a broad class of graph synthesizers (both statistical and deep-learning based) with privacy metrics, expanding evaluation dimensions to practical utility and risk, through empirical analysis of multiple actual outputs. The framework accommodates both an Exact Solution scenario, where synthesizer behavior is directly observable, and a Monte Carlo Approximation scenario where only synthetic outputs from a black box synthesizer are available. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets and seven widely used graph synthesizers demonstrate framework's versatility, enabling privacy evaluation for different attack goals (e.g., to infer an edge or node) and capabilities (e.g., observing one or multiple synthetic graphs). We analyze evaluation results by examining the relationship between graph statistics and synthesizer design choices, providing insights for data curators in PGS selection and researchers for improved PGS design.
item.dc:creator: Yu Duan, Luca Baldesi, Carter T. Butts, Athina Markopoulou

item.title: BATCH: Behavior Alignment for Cross-Embodiment Learning from Humans
item.description: Human demonstrations provide a scalable source of diverse manipulation data, but leveraging them for robot learning remains challenging due to differences in embodiment, viewpoint, action spaces, and temporal structure. We introduce BATCH, a cross-embodiment learning framework that explicitly aligns human and robot behaviors. BATCH learns self-supervised temporal representations with a cycle-consistency objective to establish cross-embodiment correspondences without manual annotation. We further introduce two complementary training objectives that leverage these correspondences within an autoregressive videoaction diffusion model: behavior-aligned co-training and human-to-robot style transfer. On real-world manipulation tasks, BATCH improves generalization to unseen task configurations compared with training on unaligned data and prior cross-embodiment baselines, with additional gains from the style-transfer objective. Our results demonstrate that explicit behavior alignment enables more effective transfer from human demonstrations to robot policies.
item.dc:creator: Zeyi Liu, Shuran Song

item.title: NINJA: A Navigator-Inspector Joint Architecture for Context-Efficient Issue Localization
item.description: Recent advances in agent-based methods have demonstrated strong promise for issue localization, a critical prerequisite for software issue resolution. However, most existing agent-based methods rely on a single agent with a growing context, where long-context accumulation compresses the effective reasoning space. Meanwhile, the flat exploration structure hinders the balance between file-level breadth and function-level depth. To address these limitations, we propose NINJA, a hierarchical Navigator-Inspector Joint Architecture for context-efficient issue localization. NINJA decomposes repository exploration into global navigation and local inspection: the navigator maintains the global search state, performs file-level search, and dispatches selected entry files, while inspectors independently conduct function-level exploration around the assigned files in separate contexts. Through multi-round interactions, inspectors return suspicious locations as feedback, and the navigator updates the global state to decide whether to continue exploration or finalize localization. This hierarchical design balances file-level breadth with function-level depth, while independent inspector contexts prevent local exploration traces from accumulating in a single growing context. To further strengthen both global coordination and local exploration, we introduce a two-stage agentic fine-tuning strategy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones show that NINJA consistently outperforms competitive baselines. Notably, after fine-tuning, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct surpasses the strong closed-source Claude-Haiku-4.5 model. Our code is available at https://github.com/wantbook-book/NINJA.
item.dc:creator: Wenkai Fang, Shunyu Liu, Wei Luo, Zihao Wu, Yang Zhou, Tongya Zheng, Wotao Yin, Jialie Shen, Leszek Rutkowski, Mingli Song, Dacheng Tao

item.title: MetaPI: Constructing Prompt Injection Benchmarks from LLM Agent Benchmark
item.description: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly perform complex tasks using high-privilege tools, making indirect prompt injection (IPI) a critical security risk. However, IPI benchmarks lag behind their rapidly evolving utility counterparts, only offering limited task and environment coverage and relying on narrow, static attack scenarios. In this paper, we propose meta-benchmarking for IPI: transforming existing utility benchmarks into end-to-end IPI evaluation suites that reuse their realistic tasks, environments, and infrastructure. We present MetaPI, an extensible toolkit that automatically identifies plausible injection points, generates realistic attack objectives, optimizes adaptive payloads, and validates attacks in the real environment. Its modular interfaces support heterogeneous environments, agents, defenses, and attack algorithms, allowing new components to be integrated without redesigning the evaluation pipeline. We apply MetaPI to AppWorld, VitaBench, and Terminal-Bench and evaluate representative agents and defenses across multiple backbone LLMs. Our results show that no evaluated defense simultaneously achieves strong utility and strong security in realistic, adaptive agentic IPI settings. MetaPI thus enables scalable and consistent security evaluation across diverse and evolving agent ecosystems
item.dc:creator: Peiran Wang, Chong Xiang, Wenjie Qu, Ying Li, Jiaheng Zhang, G. Edward Suh, Yuan Tian

item.title: Topic-Aware Multi-Task Mental Health Classification with Active Learning-Based Stepwise Relabeling for Social Media Conversations
item.description: Mental health conditions affect millions of people worldwide, yet many cases go undetected until they reach a critical stage. Social media platforms like Reddit have become spaces where people openly share their experiences, but the support is often provided by individuals without clinical training. Existing multi-task approaches jointly model emotion and sentiment for mental health classification but frequently rely on noisy labels generated by pre-trained models and overlook topic information as a useful signal. This paper introduces two key contributions: First, an existing Core Fusion Network framework is extended by adding Topic alongside existing Mental Health Condition, Emotion, and Sentiment Classification tasks, with topic labels derived from the therapist-client interactions in the CounselChat dataset. Second, an Active Learning-based Stepwise Relabeling approach is proposed to refine a small subset of noisy emotion and topic labels using pre-trained models in two stages: targeting medium-uncertainty samples first, followed by high-uncertainty samples. The predictions above a confidence threshold (0.7) are accepted to prevent error propagation. The experiments are conducted on the SuicideWatch and Mental Health dataset of 54,412 Reddit posts collected from five mental health subreddits, evaluating domain-specific transformer encoders including MentalBERT and MentalRoBERTa. The proposed Active Learning-based Stepwise Relabeling, when applied to Core Fusion Network with MentalRoBERTa, improves Mental Health Condition by 0.09%, Emotion by 0.51%, Sentiment by 0.35%, and Topic Classification by 1.57% over the baseline Core Fusion Network. The results suggest that the proposed framework significantly reduces label noise in multi-task mental health classification, and that topic information provides additional context.
item.dc:creator: Revathy Iswarya Sekaran, Vansh Bhardwaj, Aveek Sahana, Utkarshani Jaimini

item.title: Causal Discovery Bench: Can LLMs Autonomously Conduct Effective Experiments?
item.description: As large language model (LLM) agents get actively adopted for autonomous research, they must not only reason over existing evidence, but also design informative experiments, allocate resources, analyze sequential observations, and decide when to stop and make conclusions. Yet these capabilities remain poorly measured. We introduce Causal-Discovery-Bench (https://github.com/mshen1019/causal-discovery-bench), a verifiable sandbox with configurable structural equation models and resource constraints to evaluate sequential experimental design and causal discovery without domain-semantic cues. Across 3,802 episodes with 13 models from 5 vendors, we analyze agent behavior along 40 metrics in seven families. Agents' performance exhibits a four-level difficulty hierarchy spanning single-experiment design, sequential exploration of causal relationships, resource-aware experimentation balancing cost and statistical power, and autonomous resolution of conflicting evidence. We identify a substantial performance gap between causal inference from correctly curated evidence and navigating causal discovery through autonomous experimentation: Analyzing agents' action trajectories attributes 94.5% of their mistakes to experimental design rather than to inference, which is further consolidated with ablation studies. Relaxing resource constraints alone does not reliably resolve failures in sequential discovery. In contrast, basic statistical tools substantially improve performance across multiple model families, while advanced tools provide little additional benefit when models lack prerequisite lower-level capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Zhuoyang Liu, Ning Peng, Ming Shen, Zijun Gao

item.title: Personalized Alignment of Language Models with Human Value Profiles
item.description: Large language models are increasingly used for subjective tasks such as seeking advice, where there is often no single correct answer. Yet dominant alignment methods learn a single behavior policy that applies uniformly across users, limiting their ability to reflect individual value priorities. We propose personalized value alignment, a framework for adapting model responses to users' stable value profiles rather than to personas, demographics, or task-specific preferences used in prior personalization work. Our approach represents users through Schwartz value profiles and selects which of their values are relevant to each query before applying targeted prompting, activation steering, or LoRA-DPO. We create a dataset of 1,501 value-tension scenarios and evaluate over 152 diverse value profiles sampled from a nationally representative survey. Value-targeted methods outperform no-personalization, demographic, and full-profile prompting baselines, indicating that gains come from focused conditioning on query-specific value priorities rather than mere exposure. We further find that steering effects are not uniform across users: alignment gains vary by where a user's priorities fall in the value space. Combining targeted prompting with activation steering or LoRA-DPO yields the strongest personalization while keeping logical quality within adequate range.
item.dc:creator: Rashon Poole, Farnaz Jahanbakhsh

item.title: MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning
item.description: AI systems must often maintain bounded memory of unbounded interaction histories. However, optimizing the memory representation, and its updates, for downstream task utility is difficult for standard reinforcement learning (RL) due to severe credit assignment bottlenecks induced by sparse, delayed rewards. We introduce MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory), a framework that formulates incremental summarization as a capacity-constrained, information-theoretic reward-shaping problem. Grounded in value suboptimality bounds, we show that bounding sequential information loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant targets, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency. We introduce a recursive consistency condition to ensure summaries are grounded by maximizing mutual information (MI) with the observed history. We mitigate credit assignment issues with a parameterized asymmetric critic that computes step-wise variational MI bounds for dense reward shaping. Empirical evaluation on long-horizon scientific reading and multi-turn dialogue benchmarks shows that MaxIM outperforms RL, supervised fine-tuning, and prompt-focused baselines on factual grounding, comprehensive autorater metrics, and downstream task utility across strict token budgets and extended horizons, without the need for expensive human preference labels.
item.dc:creator: Jihwan Jeong, Guy Tennenholtz, Yinlam Chow, Chih-Wei Hsu, Craig Boutilier

item.title: LogCDM: Interpretable Log Anomaly Detection via Behavioral Graph Drift and Adaptive Signal Fusion
item.description: Log-based anomaly detection is increasingly dominated by large pretrained models, from BERT-scale encoders to 8B-parameter language models, which require GPUs at inference time and are difficult to deploy on the monitoring nodes where logs are produced. We present LogCDM, a compact detector that scores each log session using three complementary signals: the next-event surprise of a small causal Transformer, the distance between a graph-attention embedding of the session's own transition graph and that of a normal reference graph, and a transition-drift statistic that we show is exactly a frequency-weighted chi-squared divergence between transition kernels. The divergence view yields an asymptotic null distribution, a length-standardized score, and a per-edge decomposition that explains each alarm. A sigmoid gate fuses the three signals; under a shared-covariance Gaussian model, this gate is the Bayes posterior, and its learned weights indicate which signal each dataset relies on. With 8.1-8.8M parameters and no GPU required at inference, LogCDM reaches F1 scores of 0.984 on HDFS, 0.870 on chronologically split BGL, and 0.850 on Thunderbird, within 0.013-0.12 of an 8.1B-parameter LLM detector evaluated under the same protocol and above all compact baselines on BGL. It scores a session in 5.5-10.5 ms on a CPU. Ablations show that the structural signals add 0.025-0.030 F1 on BGL and Thunderbird but almost nothing on HDFS, consistent with the learned fusion weights.
item.dc:creator: Suryansh Talukdar, Taha Sarwat, Jin Soung Yoo

item.title: AutoBuddy: Evaluating Proactive, Always-On Agents on Task Discovery and Execution in a Simulated Workplace
item.description: As LLM agents become more autonomous, they are increasingly expected to run as always-on assistants on a user's behalf, identifying work to be done and completing it without being asked. Yet existing benchmarks usually give the agent its task, whereas in knowledge work the requests sit in the user's workspace and the agent must first recognise which obligations exist. We study proactive task discovery and execution, in which an agent must infer a user's pending tasks from their workspace and complete them in the systems where the work lives. This setting poses two challenges. For the agent, the tasks are buried in a large volume of mail, chat, documents and records. For evaluation, a benchmark needs a simulated organisation whose people, events and documents are mutually consistent, so that tasks arise realistically and their correct outcomes are known. We introduce AutoBuddy-Bench, a simulator that addresses these challenges. It models an organisation's employees, projects, business systems and event history as a temporal graph, renders it into realistic workspace artefacts, derives ground-truth tasks from the events that create obligations, and computes each task's outcome from the world state; execution is judged by the agent's changes to the workspace. To evaluate current LLMs, we build AutoBuddy, a reference agent with interchangeable backbone LLMs: it identifies tasks from the workspace, grounding each in its source records, and executes each in a separate session with write access. Varying only the backbone, we find a systematic shift in where tasks are lost: weaker models fail mainly at discovery, intermediate models identify tasks but often stop short of carrying them out, and the strongest models fail mainly during execution, most often on business-system operations. Discovery precision is only weakly related to execution quality, suggesting the two are distinct capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Shiqi Chen, Daniel Madrigal Diaz, Wei-Ning Chen, Gbola Afonja, Fangkai Yang, Rujia Wang, Chetan Bansal, Victor R\"uhle, Saravan Rajmohan, Dongge Han

item.title: SkillDuet: Co-Evolving Models and Skills through Response Feedback
item.description: During reinforcement learning, experience can be both internalized in LLM parameters and retained externally as reusable textual skills. Parameter updates alter the model's behavior and the interaction experience from which new skills are extracted. These skills, in turn, guide the model's subsequent interactions and parameter updates. As the model's capabilities evolve, previously beneficial skills may become redundant or detrimental. We present SkillDuet, a framework that coordinates parameter updates and skill evolution through model response feedback. Skills extracted from on-policy trajectories guide parameter updates through OPD at every step. A response-based score, Strength, ranks candidate skills by the magnitude of the shift they induce in the current model's responses, and the highest-scoring skills are periodically consolidated into a persistent global skill set (Global). The updated model and Global jointly guide subsequent interactions, generating experience for further parameter and skill updates. With Qwen3-4B, SkillDuet achieves success rates of 98.57% on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, exceeding the matched SEED-API baseline by 2.86 and 5.47 percentage points, respectively. Ablations show that response-based skill selection and Global consolidation improve task performance. Further experiments show that the benefits of retained skills depend on both their content and their compatibility with the model. SkillDuet provides a concrete mechanism for model-skill co-evolution and skill-level recursive self-improvement.
item.dc:creator: Xingguang Ji, Ziqiang Dong, Yubo Zhang, Xi Leng, Yang Yang, Guanjun Jiang

item.title: From Fluent Text to Ontology-Compatible Definitions: A Quality-Control Agentic Workflow
item.description: Biomedical ontologies are structured knowledge systems that must evolve continuously to represent newly emerging knowledge, but their manual maintenance remains time-consuming and laborintensive. Textual definitions are especially costly because they must be readable to humans and compatible with controlled entities, relations, and logical constraints. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising way to assist ontology engineering tasks, including definition generation. However, textual plausibility does not guarantee knowledge-system compatibility. A generated definition may be fluent and close to a reference definition, yet still fail to ground its implied entities or violate ontology-level constraints. Directly inserting such definitions into ontology libraries may therefore introduce entity-level hallucinations and logical inconsistencies. To address this problem, we propose two structured-knowledge incompatibility metrics, Entity Error Rate (EER) and Logical Inconsistency Rate (LIR), to quantify entity grounding and logical consistency for LLM-generated ontology definitions. We further develop an agentic quality-control (QC) workflow that treats definition generation as an iterative process rather than a direct decoding step: it generates definitions, extracts axioms, checks entity existence and logical consistency, and uses the resulting diagnostics to drive repair loops. Comprehensive experiments on Disease Ontology, Uberon Ontology, and Uberon-ConstraintStress demonstrate that EER and LIR complement conventional reference-based metrics by evaluating whether generated content can be grounded and checked inside the target ontology. The workflow effectively decreases EER while maintaining strong conventional text-generation performance. LIR further exposes sparse ontology-level logical failures that are invisible to text similarity metrics, although their repair remains limited.
item.dc:creator: Kun Feng, Chenchen Chu, Yan Liu, Haojie Sun, Jijun Tang, Chen Tian, Shuolin Xiao, Jianping He, Zhao Li

item.title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
item.description: In this work, we study whether frontier agent can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from 6.82% with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to 19.86%. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, Our Infrathon framework provide resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions.
item.dc:creator: Zhengyu Hu, Zheyuan Xiao, Yike Wang, Hamish Ivison, Haoyu Wang, Yige Yuan, Rulin Shao, Yuetai Li, Niqi Lyu, Yicheng Ding, Shu Yang, Zhichen Zeng, Banghua Zhu, Jiaxin Pei, Kaize Ding, Pradeep Dasigi, Dan Roth, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Noah A. Smith, Teng Xiao, Radha Poovendran

item.title: When Should AI Overturn a Human Decision? Controversy at the 2026 World Cup and a $\sqrt{2/\pi}$ Solution
item.description: We study how to combine a human binary call (a referee's offside or onside decision) with an AI numerical measurement (VAR's estimate of an attacker's position relative to the offside line). We derive an explicit maximum-likelihood rule that determines when the referee's call should stand and when a conflicting VAR measurement should overturn it. Our model treats the true offside margin as fixed and unknown and assumes independent additive Gaussian errors in the human's perception and the AI measurement. When both errors have zero means and known standard deviations $\sigma_H$ and $\sigma_{AI}$, respectively, the reversal threshold is $\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\sigma^2_{AI}/\sigma_H$. An onside call is overturned precisely when VAR's measured offside margin exceeds this threshold---not merely because VAR places the attacker beyond the offside line. We also derive the rule when either source has a systematic bias. We prove that the maximum-likelihood estimate of the true margin exists and is unique, while the final binary decision requires only a threshold comparison, without computing that estimate numerically. We illustrate the rule through numerical examples and show how to estimate the error parameters from calibration data. The same analysis applies beyond soccer to binary classification problems in which a human call and an AI measurement satisfy the stated model. This paper is intended for educational purposes: we aim to illustrate how undergraduate students and advanced high school students familiar with basic probability and calculus can investigate research questions in AI and its applications.
item.dc:creator: Amir Ali Ahmadi, Parsa Alavi, Radeen Alavi

item.title: State Media at Retrieval Time: A Large-Scale Audit of Russian State-Aligned Sources in AI Chatbot Responses
item.description: The Pravda Network is a Russian state-aligned media aggregator, with over 110 websites and more than 15 million articles published since 2023. Given its prolific and repetitive output, emerging scholarship argues that the Pravda Network was built to influence AI systems. We conduct a large-scale audit of leading AI chatbots to understand: (1) the retrieval rates of Pravda Network articles, (2) the conditions of retrieval, and (3) whether chatbot responses affirm or caveat this content. We build a 10,000 prompt corpus from sampled Pravda Network headlines varied along two dimensions (headline rewording and user skepticism) and query 11 AI chatbots via the web interface (n=104,997 completed responses). Overall, we find susceptibility to Pravda Network retrieval to be infrequent---appearing in 7.3% of responses---and highly platform dependent---with three chatbots responsible for 94% of retrievals (You.com, Claude, and Copilot). Among the frontier models, Claude is an outlier: ChatGPT, Gemini, and Meta AI retrieved no Pravda Network articles, likely indicative of a domain-level filtering policy. All 11 chatbots, however, retrieved other Russian state-aligned media to some degree (median=13.56% of responses). When Pravda Network articles are surfaced, caveat rates vary widely by platform (from 5.3% to 76.2%), with You.com providing the fewest caveats. We also identify the tactic of headline washing: where 9.92% of sampled Pravda Network headlines attribute their reporting to other, often more credible, media outlets, while the articles themselves are republished from Russian state-aligned media. We discuss headline washing's potential to launder state media as independent reporting. With this audit, we provide a systematic analysis of AI chatbots' susceptibility to Russia's latest attempt to manipulate the information environment.
item.dc:creator: Laura Kurek, Elijah Covert, Rafael I Bonilla, Eric Gilbert, Ceren Budak

item.title: CASCoDe: A Closed-Loop Agentic Framework for Analog Sizing and Layout Co-Design
item.description: Expert analog layouts differ from auto-generated ones in density and regularity, not only in legality: experts make a succession of discrete, hierarchical physical decisions and revisit each after extracted electrical results, while most existing automated flows act on a physical search space fixed before the controller runs. We present CASCoDe, a closed-loop LLM agent framework for analog netlist-to-layout design that formalizes those expert decisions as a hierarchical discrete action space-sizing selection, structural floorplan, local layout refinement, routing-attempt selection-on which the agent runs feedback-driven tree search from a circuit netlist to a verified GDS. The agent authors the circuit-specific floorplans and scripts, and an execution layer of interface adaptations over adapted tools make every action land at physical implementation and be judged by DRC, LVS, and extracted-RC simulation. On 20 SKY130 amplifiers spanning single-, two-, and three-stage topologies, CASCoDe is the only flow that delivers a DRC- and LVS-clean routed layout when meeting design specifications for every circuit. It reduces area by 59-85% (mean 71%) against a conventional P&R flow on identical PCells, raises mean device density from 0.39 to 0.74 against APPlace, MAGICAL, ALIGN and ICPI. A layout that beats every baseline in area and legality appears after 11 minutes of agent time on average, and ablations show that the structured action space and the feedback-guided tree search each reduce area and search cost.
item.dc:creator: Ziming Wei, Bingyang Liu, David Z. Pan

item.title: Measuring Generative AI Content in Political Campaigns: Evidence of Rising Adoption and Non-Disclosure
item.description: The use of generative AI in political campaigns has drawn public concern and policy attention. Public concerns range from distrust of candidates to skepticism about the authenticity and accuracy of political advertising, including AI-generated images and video. Nearly half of U.S. states have enacted laws that prohibit, or require disclosure of, "materially deceptive" AI-generated content (AIGC) in elections to guard against these concerns. This study measures how candidates and their campaigns produce and circulate AIGC during an election cycle. We develop two measures that estimate not only wether campaigns use AIGC, but how much they produce (magnitude) and in what forms (modality). We apply these measures to a novel dataset of text and images from the campaign websites, X accounts, and emails of 12,977 candidates for U.S. political office from 2023 to 2025. We report three findings. First, detectable AIGC from campaigns increased significantly across modalities over the observation window, and campaigns that use AIGC frequently do not disclose it. Second, incumbents' campaigns produced significantly less AIGC than challengers' campaigns. Third, candidates in states with AIGC disclosure or prohibition laws do not produce measurably less AIGC than candidates in other states. Our method and findings have implications for transparency and trust in elections, and on state laws that regulate AI use in campaigns. Because current state laws largely target mainly "materially deceptive" content, we identify additional policy mechanisms that could increase electoral transparency and improve trust as AIGC becomes more prevalent.
item.dc:creator: Anna-Maria Gueorguieva, Nic Weber

item.title: Inside the Trading Loop: Markets, Models, and Moves with LLM Agents
item.description: We built a hybrid multi-agent trading system that combines large language model (LLM) analysts with momentum-based portfolio construction and rule-based execution. Company-news and macroeconomic agents return structured reports to a coordinator that sets stock weights and cash reserves. We evaluate the portfolio engine using its broker-recorded paper account, which operated with deterministic fallbacks, and compare LLM-enabled configurations through retrospective replays. From March 11 to August 28, 2026, the account returned 34.5%, compared with 14.4% for the S&P 500 fund SPY over the same dates. This raw return advantage came with a larger maximum drawdown. Reconstructed policies also finish above matched SPY and QQQ references when assessments are used in the same session or deferred to the next. Design comparisons examine cash authority, selective invocation, and response contracts. A constant-cash control gives a return estimate close to stance-based sizing, and shorter report contracts improve observed parsing but can change recommendations.
item.dc:creator: Renee Jia, Di Mu, Yao Yu, Tianrui Liu

item.title: Improving Analytic Constants via Interpretable AI-Guided Lean Proof Refinement
item.description: AI agents are increasingly capable of discovering new mathematical results, yet their reasoning and generated proofs can be difficult to understand and verify. We introduce an interpretable framework for AI-guided mathematical discovery, focused on improving quantitative bounds on analytic constants. Our key insight is that existing proofs often contain slack in intermediate lemmas, which can be tightened without reconstructing the entire argument. To exploit this structure, we represent proofs as partially-formalized Lean blueprints: human-interpretable dependency graphs of definitions, lemmas, and theorems. An AI agent then iteratively refines the Lean code while preserving the blueprint's dependency structure, allowing local improvements to automatically propagate to a verified final bound. This interpretable structure allows humans to inspect the agent's refinements and understand how local improvements propagate to the final theorem. For Grothendieck's constant ($\mathcal{K}_G$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_G \leq \frac{\pi}{2\log(1+\sqrt{2})} - 10^{-17}, $$ an explicit numerical improvement over Krivine's 1977 bound. For Korenblum's constant ($\mathcal{K}_K$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_K \geq 0.356565, $$ improving Wang's 2025 bound of $0.3554$. Our experiments demonstrate the potential of both partial formalization and iterative agentic refinement for interpretable mathematical discovery.
item.dc:creator: Rahul Saha, Alan Li, Anton Xue, Swarat Chaudhuri, Adam Klivans, Pravesh K. Kothari, Raghu Meka

item.title: A Gamified Framework for Conflict-Driven Design: Discovering Strategies for Collaborative Resilience with Multi-Agent Learning
item.description: Conflicting stakeholder objectives make it difficult to coordinate investments in urban resilience. We model conflict-driven urban design as a non-zero-sum digital board game in which stakeholder agents allocate scarce resources and balance individual payoffs against shared urban development and resilience objectives. We use multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to train policies and examine their behavior across three settings. On a 4 x 4 board, learned policies reach about 84% of the total return found by a simulated annealing benchmark. On an 8 x 8 board with spatial and resource constraints, trained agents favor projects that improve resilience in self-play. In a 12 x 12 simulation initialized from historical maps of Tatsumi, Tokyo, trained agents achieve a mean total score of 452.1, compared with 357.3 for a random-policy baseline across 10,000 simulation runs. Gains in adaptability, sustainability, flood resistance, and greenery come with reductions in vitality and density. A human-in-the-loop interface supports replay and lets participants take over stakeholder decisions, providing a testbed for exploring these trade-offs in participatory urban planning.
item.dc:creator: Jin Gao

item.title: Efficient LLM Adaptation with Forward-Only Passes
item.description: Large language model (LLM) inference serving is undergoing rapid growth and large-scale deployment, motivating us to rethink how the inference process itself can be leveraged to enable efficient task-specific LLM adaptation. In this paper, we propose a forward-only approach for efficient LLM adaptation with forward-only passes in LLM inference serving. We exploit the angle concentration of activations induced by each singular value decomposition (SVD) component to measure its contribution-dispersed or concentrated-to the angle concentration of the hidden states. Based on this, our forward-only search then efficiently identifies the weight matrix with the highest dispersion that merits rank reduction. We then selectively remove the higher-order components and retain the lower-order components in SVD. Empirical results across diverse datasets demonstrate the competitive accuracy of our forward-only approach, while theoretical analysis shows lower peak memory and greater speedup than the gradient-based approach and greater speedup than the exhaustive search approach. The experiments further present the robustness and generalization of our forward-only approach to various LLMs with up to 57B parameters. The code is included in the supplementary material.
item.dc:creator: Baichuan Huang, Ananth Balashankar, Amir Aminifar

item.title: In Search of Lost Time: Temporal Competence in Large Language Models
item.description: Today's large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with time: AI agents schedule tasks, coordinate with people and other AI systems, and even decide how long to think. Yet LLMs only ever encounter time secondhand---in descriptions rather than experience. Does this hinder their reasoning and decisions that involve time? Our paper traces this question from a model's knowledge to its actions through four successive evaluations. We find that models know the rules of time, which can be read, but struggle to predict durations, which must be lived; while they are highly accurate (92.0-97.5\%) on a collection of questions built from the theorems of various time-related literatures, they underestimate their own completion times by up to 99.5\% and fail to identify which tasks will take them longer to run. And while they are better at estimating durations of human tasks, their duration judgments change based on how an event is worded, magnifying similar human biases by up to 1.3$\times$. Moving from estimation to action, we find that some LLMs disregard time costs completely when answering user queries, ignoring a 1,200-fold increase in wait time entirely. Together, our experiments reveal new challenges posed to LLMs as they navigate a dimension they cannot directly perceive, and highlight how their blind spots can even be simple cognitive abilities that humans take for granted.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Liu, David Lee, Icey Siyi Ai, Marwa Abdulhai, Rachit Dubey, Thomas L. Griffiths

item.title: IdealCache: Rethinking Cache Scheduling in Diffusion Transformers via Ideal Trajectories
item.description: Feature caching accelerates Diffusion Transformers by reusing intermediate computations across denoising timesteps, yet existing methods share a fundamental blind spot: they treat the standard reference denoising trajectory as the optimisation target, approximating its per-step states and thus inheriting its output as an implicit quality ceiling. We argue that this target is arbitrary -- what truly matters is the ideal result, not the intermediate path taken to reach it. We propose IdealCache, a training-free framework that abandons step-wise imitation of the reference trajectory. Instead, it anchors caching on a per-input ensemble of ideal trajectories constructed from candidate target results, aggregates their geometry into a single graph, and discovers optimal non-uniform schedules via a constrained shortest path on this graph. By decoupling from the reference process, IdealCache breaks the performance bottleneck of trajectory-approximation; our schedules can attain near-lossless fidelity in generation and even surpass on task-specific metrics (e.g., maintaining higher semantic consistency in image editing). Without retraining, IdealCache achieves 6.35x speedup on Qwen-Image, 5.84x on Qwen-Image-Edit, and 4.32x on HunyuanVideo, with competitive or superior quality across tasks.
item.dc:creator: Shang Xue, Li Zhu, Ping Chen

item.title: Conformal Fair Decoding for Large Language Model Recommenders
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) can generate personalized recommendations without task-specific training, but changing a protected attribute while holding interaction history fixed can alter the semantic content of recommended items. We study fairness control when model weights and full-vocabulary logits are unavailable. We propose Fair- Rec, an item-level decoding framework that uses an offline-calibrated semantic-disparity threshold and controls candidate selection as recommendation lists are generated. A hard variant filters candidates against the threshold; a soft variant trades off candidate likelihood and disparity while adapting a penalty using observed violations. Under an explicit uniform enforceability assumption, we establish a pathwise O(1/T) upper bound on the excess empirical violation rate of the soft decoder. Experiments on MovieLens-1M and Amazon Movies & TV using Qwen3-8B and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct show that the soft variant lowers measured counterfactual disparity relative to zero- =shot recommendation, UP5, and FACTER, while retaining competitive HR@10 and NDCG@10.
item.dc:creator: Ziwei Wu, Jingrui He

item.title: Adversarial Evaluation of Large Language Models for Patient-Friendly Radiology Report Summarization
item.description: Purpose: To develop and validate a scalable adversarial evaluation framework for assessing the robustness of large language models (LLMs) that generate patient-friendly summaries of radiology reports. Methods: We introduced a clinically grounded adversarial framework that uses controlled term substitutions and impression removals across intensity levels. Using a radiologist-validated adversarial dictionary, we generated adversarial variants of CT and MRI reports. Six LLMs summarized original and adversarial impressions using 2 prompt styles, yielding 18,000 evaluation pairs. Robustness was evaluated with an automated LLM-as-a-judge framework scoring factual faithfulness, sensitivity to adversarial edits, certainty fidelity, and hallucination rate. Failure mode analysis quantified vulnerabilities in incorporating clinical modifiers. Agreement with two radiologists was assessed on 105 cases. Results: GPT-5-mini achieved the highest factual faithfulness and certainty fidelity under both adversarial edits. Under term substitution, hallucinations occurred in 28.1-30.1% of GPT-5-mini summaries, compared with 35.3-36.4% for Claude Sonnet 4.5 and 41.4-41.9% for MedGemma. Impression-removal edits were handled more robustly than term substitutions. Even for the highest-scoring summarizer, substitutions of anatomical terms were not reflected in 23.7% of summaries, diagnostic certainty in 22.3%, and descriptor terms (e.g., "substantial") in 21.2%. Judge-radiologist agreement (macro-F1: 0.55-0.56) was comparable to inter-radiologist agreement (0.53). Conclusions: Adversarial evaluation exposes clinically meaningful failure modes, including missed anatomical modifiers, altered diagnostic certainty, and omitted severity descriptors.
