item.dc:creator: Magdalini Paschali, Asad Aali, Arogya Koirala, Andrew Johnston, Katherine McNamara, Richard Gaus, Roxana Daneshjou, David B. Larson, Akshay S. Chaudhari

item.title: AVCORP: Identifying and Resisting Deception via Communication Theory and Theory of Mind
item.description: Today's LLM-based agents are vulnerable to deception by users and other agents. Defending against deception requires Theory of Mind (ToM) reasoning to infer the beliefs and goals of others as well as modeling tactics based on communication theory. To enable training models to detect deception, we adopt the well-known deception game, Avalon. We present a corpus, AVCORP, of 5,000 annotated utterances from 250 games of Avalon. AVCORP includes (1) 37 tactics mapped to a 4x4 behavior matrix, and (2) reasoning traces capturing abductive hypotheses, suspicion levels, and nested ToM beliefs. We train Qwen3-8B on AVCORP and evaluate it on 25 held-out games and 20 games played by humans. On held-out games, our best trained detector outperforms its untrained baseline and frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro), matching Claude Opus 5.5. On human games, every trained detector exceeds the untrained model in F1 score across all rounds.
item.dc:creator: Fardin Saad, Zhe Zhang, Sanjana Cheerla, Amanul Haque, Munindar P. Singh

item.title: Homeopathic Learning: Diluting poisoned fine-tuning data can strengthen its effect
item.description: We study homeopathic learning, a phenomenon where poisoned training data with little effect on its own can create a hidden backdoor once clean, contrasting data is added. In our experiments, a model fine-tuned only on a "poison" dataset associated with a trait T (such as speaking German or being misaligned) does not learn T. Surprisingly, adding similarly formatted "clean" data not associated with T causes the model to learn T. This effect requires that the poison data have an identifying "trigger" feature that is absent from the clean data. We demonstrate this effect in a variety of settings: subliminal learning of backdoor behaviors, inoculation prompting of reward hacking transcripts, generalization from archaic bird names, and an MNIST classifier with mislabeled data. We propose a simple regression model as an explanation. In the poison data, the task and trigger always co-occur, and regularization favors attributing T to the task. Clean data without the trigger causes T to be attributed to the trigger instead. Consequently, the same training examples can have little effect as part of one training set but create a misalignment backdoor in another. This finding exposes a potential limitation of safety methods that audit or filter training data in isolation.
item.dc:creator: Matt Clarke, Jan Dubi\'nski, James Chua, Simon Schrodi, Owain Evans, Alex Cloud

item.title: The Infrastructure Divide: Analyzing Community Stance on Data Center Development via Reddit
item.description: The rapid expansion of AI-driven data center construction has outpaced public engagement: an estimated $64 billion in U.S. data center projects were blocked or delayed by local opposition between May 2024 and March 2025, yet the concerns driving this resistance remain poorly characterized. Prior engagement methods such as surveys and hearings are introduced late in the planning process, and no study has systematically mined social media to measure community stance at scale. To address this gap, this study presents an LLM-powered opinion-mining framework and applies it to 798 Reddit posts and 102,328 associated comments spanning a decade. An open-source large language model, guided by a Chain-of-Stance prompting framework and three domain-specific labeling rules, classified stance at 83% of the human inter-reviewer agreement ceiling. Opposition dominated discourse volume rather than disapproval: against posts outnumbered favor posts 2.6:1 and generated 8.5 times more comments, and this gap widened significantly over 86 weeks. Topic modeling of opposition arguments resolved into four reproducible clusters, resource consumption and scarcity (42.8%), contested siting processes and secrecy (34.2%), political opposition to data centers (13%), and political and corporate accountability (8%). Engagement analysis revealed that posts with emotional or provocative political framing attracted the most engagement, while key technical concerns (e.g., water, power) were dispersed across lower-engagement comment threads. These findings give local leaders, developers, and policy makers a quantified, continuously updatable basis for prioritizing concerns and policy levers, supporting a shift from opposition to negotiated, verifiable partnership for data center development.
item.dc:creator: Yoko Koyama, Gongfan Chen, Mansi Saxena

item.title: AYO: A Safe and Privacy-Preserving Platform for Studying Children's Interaction with LLMs
item.description: Children and adolescents are increasingly interacting with generative AI and large language models (LLMs), yet little is known about how these interactions may influence their development, beliefs, and behavior. Existing research has relied heavily on surveys, while direct study of children's interactions with LLMs presents substantial challenges related to safety, privacy, consent, and experimental control. We introduce AYO (AI Youth Open Science), an open-source platform designed for safe and systematic research on children's interactions with conversational AI. AYO provides a child-friendly interface, configurable age-based safety guardrails, researcher monitoring, and privacy-preserving data practices. These capabilities enable cross-sectional, longitudinal, and experimental research on how children use and respond to LLMs and how AI design may shape trust, epistemic judgment, curiosity, and other aspects of development. AYO provides the infrastructure to generate evidence that guides safer AI systems, educational practices, and policies for children growing up with AI.
item.dc:creator: Huiwen Alex Yang, Rachel Skwersky, Bill D. Thompson, Celeste Kidd

item.title: LoRazor: Trimming Adapter Execution for Efficient Multi-LoRA Serving
item.description: LoRA offers a parameter-efficient adaptation strategy, supporting multi-user workloads via customized adapters on a shared backbone. However, serving concurrent requests with different adapters introduces substantial computation and memory-management overhead. We ask the research question: Do all requests need their adapters throughout the whole generation process? Our motivational study reveals that employing LoRA adapters at every decoding step is unnecessary, releasing them early has limited impact on accuracy while substantially accelerating generation. Although skipping adapters early offers theoretical workload reduction, translating these computational savings into concrete throughput gains requires tailored GPU kernels. We present LoRazor, a multi-LoRA serving framework that combines early adapter release with active-row aware GPU kernels. LoRazor determines when to permanently release a request's adapter and continue decoding with the backbone alone. By dynamically resizing LoRA kernel launches as adapters are released, LoRazor trims idle GPU blocks. Across two backbones and four tasks, LoRazor achieves up to 3.02x request throughput and 2.53x output-token throughput over vLLM multi-LoRA, with a mean relative task-accuracy decrease of 2.89%.
item.dc:creator: Xiang Li, Pengcheng Wang, Azam Ikram, Saurabh Bagchi

item.title: Don't Blame The Preferences: Examining The Emergence of Sycophancy in LLM Training
item.description: AI sycophancy, the tendency of large language models (LLMs) to flatter users and affirm their beliefs, can undermine accuracy and contribute to misinformation, dependence, and overconfidence. Although prior work has benchmarked sycophancy in released models and proposed mitigations, its origins during training remain poorly understood. Preference alignment methods such as RLHF and DPO are often blamed, but their effects are rarely compared with earlier training stages. We investigate sycophancy across the training pipelines of three model families and three benchmarks. We find that sycophancy is largely established by the end of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), rather than introduced by preference alignment. Across all nine model benchmark combinations, SFT checkpoints attain at least 92% of preference aligned models' sycophancy scores and at least 85% of final models' scores; on average, they are about as sycophantic as final models. Preference alignment increases sycophancy in only four of nine cases, by an average of 4.2 percentage points when it does. To probe the underlying causes, we isolate model representations associated with sycophancy using mechanistic interpretability and measure their activation on training datasets from each stage. SFT datasets show roughly the same average activation as other training data but contribute substantially more examples, and the highest-scoring individual datasets all come from SFT. Our findings suggest that addressing sycophancy requires interventions throughout the training pipeline, particularly in data selection and augmentation for pre-training and SFT.
item.dc:creator: Chao Peter Yang, Catherine Zehr, Pranav Bijith, Brandon Fain

item.title: Local Inference for High-dimensional Time Series
item.description: Local stationarity provides a natural framework for time series whose dependence structure evolves smoothly over time. In high-dimensional settings, however, its classical definition can break down, as approximation errors accumulate across time-varying coefficients. To address this limitation, we introduce $(\epsilon_n,\delta)$-stationarity, a generalization of local stationarity that holds locally in time and allows approximation errors to grow with the dimension, and we combine it with local sparsity, which lets the set of relevant predictors change over time. We show that, for high-dimensional time-varying autoregressions, the rate of stationary approximation is driven by local sparsity, so that local sparsity governs not only estimation but also the stationary approximation itself. We then develop a \textit{local lasso} with time-varying penalties that selects relevant predictors and their periods of activity, and we derive error bounds that depend on the local sparsity, quantify the cost of nonstationarity, and guide penalty and bandwidth selection. For inference, we propose a desparsified local lasso based on local nodewise regressions and establish a linear representation with an explicit smoothing bias. Asymptotic normality then follows under two bandwidth conditions, one for coefficient variation and one for nonstationarity. Simulations and applications to macroeconomic and neuroscience data illustrate the methods.
item.dc:creator: Julien Bodelet, Davide La Vecchia, Johannes Lederer, Oliver Y. Ch\'en
